text: A small crescent of polished metal worn at the throat by infantry officers, the last survival of plate armour. By 1832 it was purely a badge of rank, so the man who calls on the insurgents to lay down their arms is marked out as the officer commanding the assault.
quote: an officer in a gorget extended his sword

term: Municipal Guards, soldiers of the line and National Guards from the suburbs
text: The three kinds of force sent against the barricades. The Municipal Guard was the professional armed police of Paris; the line regiments were the regular army; the National Guard was the citizen militia of property-owners, and the companies from the suburbs (the banlieue) had a name for being the most eager and the least disciplined. Hugo is careful throughout to say which is which.
quote: Municipal Guards, soldiers of the line and National Guards from the suburbs

text: The tall fur hats of grenadiers and of the élite companies of the National Guard. In the torchlight they are almost all the insurgents can see of the men crowning their barricade.
quote: their bearskin caps

text: Not fluff but a surgical dressing: soft fibres scraped from old linen, packed into wounds before cotton wool came into use. Making lint was the classic task of women and non-combatants in wartime, and the barricade keeps a table for it beside the one for cartridges.
quote: the two tables reserved for lint and cartridges

text: A white cloth raised to ask for a parley; under the customs of war the bearer is not to be fired on. Combeferre means to improvise one with his handkerchief on his cane, treating the insurgents and the army as two belligerents who can exchange prisoners.
quote: go as a flag of truce

term: “En voyant Lafayette, le gendarme répète: Sauvons-nous!”
text: “Seeing Lafayette, the gendarme repeats: Let’s run for it!” A street song of the moment. The old general Lafayette, hero of 1789 and 1830, was the idol of the opposition, and the funeral of General Lamarque that set off this rising had been led by him; in the song, the police flee at the mere sight of him.
quote: En voyant Lafayette

text: A five-franc piece, the coin Marius once pressed on the starving girl by the washerwomen's boulevard and she refused. To a penniless student it was real money, several days' food; she remembers that he could not afford it.
quote: You gave me a hundred sous

text: Envelopes were not yet in common use: a letter was folded so that the outside carried the address, then closed with a wafer or a blob of wax. Cosette's note is “sealed with a woman’s elegant care”; at the barricade Marius has nothing to seal with and can only fold his paper in four, so anyone who holds it can read it.
quote: Having nothing wherewith to seal this letter

text: The formal French way of addressing a letter, repeating the title: the first “Monsieur” is the salutation, the second goes with the name. “At M. Courfeyrac’s” means care of Courfeyrac, with whom Marius had been lodging.
quote: To Monsieur, Monsieur Marius Pontmercy

text: A village on the west coast of the Cotentin peninsula in Normandy. Toussaint's stammer and her country speech place her as a Norman peasant woman, and Hugo makes her lack of curiosity the whole of her value as a servant.
quote: her peasant dialect of Barneville

text: Ink dried slowly, so writers pressed a fresh page against a sheet of absorbent blotting paper kept in a little book; the blotter took a reversed copy of the words. A mirror reverses them back: geometry's “symmetrical image”. It is the most ordinary of household objects that undoes Valjean.
quote: what is called in geometry, “the symmetrical image;”

text: A short stone bollard set at the foot of a wall or the corner of a doorway to keep cartwheels from scraping the house. Parisians sat on them as on a bench. Valjean's post at his door in the Rue de l’Homme Armé becomes his place of vigil.
quote: he sat upon the stone post at the door of his house

text: Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis, the domed Jesuit church on the Rue Saint-Antoine at the southern edge of the Marais, the parish church of the Rue de l’Homme Armé's neighbourhood. Hugo sets its calm striking of the hour against the tocsin: “the tocsin is man; the hour is God.”
quote: the clock of Saint-Paul struck eleven

text: 1793, the year of the Terror, when the Revolution executed the king and then its own. For a frightened bourgeois of 1832, a smashed street-lamp in the night was enough to call up the guillotine and the mobs of that year.
quote: There is ‘Ninety-three’ come again.

text: Paris streets were lit by oil lanterns hung on ropes across the roadway, lit each evening by the lamplighter. Rioters broke them to darken the quarter so that troops could not see to aim; Gavroche treats it as a civic duty and scolds the street for “disobeying the regulations”.
quote: You are disobeying the regulations, my friend.

text: The national archives of France, housed in the Hôtel de Soubise, a great mansion with a colonnaded court at the end of the Rue de l’Homme Armé. Gavroche sees its columns only as material for a barricade.
quote: It’s the Archives, isn’t it?

text: Gavroche's name for the five-franc piece, a big silver coin worth a hundred sous: more money than a street boy would ever hold at once, roughly several days' wages for a labourer. Its five francs are its five “claws”; refusing it, he plays at being an incorruptible republican.
quote: Let us contemplate the tiger.

text: Gavroche's joke. In 1830 a provisional government had been proclaimed at the Hôtel de Ville while the old one fell; every insurrection after it dreamed of naming one. A note from a barricade of thirty men becomes, in his mouth, an official despatch of the new Republic.
quote: It comes from the Provisional Government.

text: A rich egg-and-butter bun. In Parisian slang “faire une brioche” meant to make a blunder, so Gavroche tells Valjean he is talking nonsense by saying he is baking brioches.
quote: bits of pastry vulgarly called brioches

text: An early chemical match-box of the 1820s and 1830s: a little bottle of phosphorus paste into which a sulphur-tipped match was dipped and then rubbed to catch fire. It was fiddly at the best of times, and Valjean needs three or four matches because his hand is shaking.
quote: the bottle of the Fumade lighter

text: A leather pouch worn on a belt holding paper cartridges, each a ball and a measure of powder wrapped together, to be torn open with the teeth and rammed down the barrel. A National Guardsman's full kit included one, and the porter has no trouble finding the pieces in the neighbourhood.
quote: a cartridge-box filled with cartridges

term: “Où vont les belles filles, lon la”
text: “Where the pretty girls go, lon la”: the nonsense refrain of a song Gavroche makes up as he runs. The first verses are a string of girls' names out of novels and the stage (Atala is Chateaubriand's Indian heroine, Pamela Richardson's); the later ones turn political, with old Paris knocking down the Louvre “where monarchy displayed itself in furbelows”.
quote: Où vont les belles filles

text: Mathieu Orfila, dean of the Paris medical faculty and the most famous toxicologist of the day, the expert witness in every poisoning trial. In Gavroche's song the girls' poison would make even Orfila tipsy.
quote: Griserait Monsieur Orfila.

term: “Le roi Charles-Dix ce jour-là, tenait mal et se décolla”
text: “King Charles X that day held on badly and came unstuck.” Charles X, last of the elder Bourbon kings, was driven out by the three days of July 1830, when Parisians forced the railings of the Louvre and the Tuileries. Gavroche's song imagines doing it again.
quote: Le roi Charles-Dix ce jour-là

text: A man from the Auvergne, the poor mountain country of central France. Auvergnats came to Paris in numbers as water-carriers, coal-heavers and street-corner porters (commissionnaires) with handcarts; they were a stock figure of the city, thrifty, strong and slow.
quote: the Auvergnat’s head was supported against the front of the cart

text: The Imprimerie Royale, the state printing works that produced laws, decrees and official publications, housed in the Hôtel de Rohan in the Marais. As a government building it had its own guard post, here manned by suburban National Guards on camp beds.
quote: There was a post at the Royal Printing Establishment.

text: Hand to nose, fingers spread and waggled forward, while slapping the back of the head: the French “pied de nez”, the equivalent of thumbing one's nose. Hugo calls it the condensed irony of the Parisian street boy.
quote: lifted his left hand to a level with his nose and thrust it forward three times

term: The councils of war and the public ministry
text: After June 1832 Paris was put under a state of siege and prisoners were tried by military courts (councils of war) until the highest court ruled this illegal. The “public ministry” is the state prosecutor. Hugo's joke is that the only captive of Gavroche's raid is a drunk Auvergnat, solemnly prosecuted as an accomplice.
quote: harassed before the councils of war as an accomplice

text: Four months after the February revolution of 1848 set up the Second Republic, the government closed the National Workshops that employed the Paris unemployed. The workers of the eastern faubourgs rose, and in four days of street war (23–26 June) the army crushed them with thousands dead. Hugo, then a deputy, was on the side of the Assembly; this chapter is his attempt to honour the men he helped to fight.
quote: the fatal insurrection of June, 1848

text: Greek terms: demos is the people as a political body; ochlocracy is rule by the mob. Hugo uses the pair to name what troubled him about June 1848: the poor in arms against a republic elected by universal suffrage, the people fighting itself.
quote: the ochlocracy rises against demos

text: Latin: “the dregs of the city, the law of the world.” Hugo gives the saying to Saint Jerome, the fourth-century translator of the Bible, as a thought about the poor from whom the apostles and martyrs came. The rhyme of fex and lex is the point: the lowest of the city become the rule of the earth.
quote: “Fex urbis, lex orbis,”

text: In June 1848 the great barricade at the mouth of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine stood on the Place de la Bastille, “the formidable place which had seen the 14th of July”. The working-class faubourg east of the Bastille had fought in every revolution since 1789, which is why Hugo piles the dates of the Revolution onto its heap of rubbish.
quote: the formidable place which had seen the 14th of July

text: In Greek myth the giants piled Mount Ossa on Mount Pelion to storm heaven. Hugo follows it with a pile of revolutionary dates: 1793 on 1789, Thermidor (the fall of Robespierre) on the 10th of August (the fall of the monarchy), Brumaire (Bonaparte's coup) and the Revolution's other turning-points, 1848 on 1830.
quote: an Ossa on Pelion of all revolutions

text: Two songs of the Revolution. The Marseillaise was the anthem of the nation and of the Republic; the Carmagnole was a dancing song of the sans-culottes, mocking the king and queen. Hugo's line means the rabble of the Revolution defying the Republic it had made.
quote: it was the Carmagnole bidding defiance to the Marseillaise

text: Cavaignac, Lamoricière and the other commanders who put down June 1848 had made their careers in the conquest of Algeria, begun in 1830. Zaatcha and Constantine were Algerian strongholds taken by storm, the soldiers boring through houses and coming over the roofs; they used the same method on the Faubourg du Temple.
quote: the strategy of the African generals

text: A heavy musket ball or a small iron cannon-ball, the size of a walnut, of the kind fired as grapeshot. The defenders of the Temple barricade fired them from home-made guns of cast-iron gas-pipe.
quote: a biscaïen was seen to ensconce itself in some closed shutter

text: Frédéric Cournet, a former naval officer, and Emmanuel Barthélemy, a worker sent to the galleys as a youth for shooting a policeman, both real leaders of June 1848. Exiled in London, they quarrelled and fought a duel in 1852 in which Barthélemy killed Cournet; in 1855 Barthélemy was hanged in London for a separate double killing. Hugo knew the story from exile.
quote: Cournet made the Saint-Antoine barricade; Barthélemy the barricade of the Temple.

text: An officer before the Temple barricade in June 1848, as Hugo tells it. His remark that the wall was made “of porcelain” is Hugo's emblem of that barricade's eerie precision; the cross the bullet breaks on his breast is his Legion of Honour.
quote: It is made of porcelain.

text: In the military language of the time, not a vehicle but a field hospital or dressing-station. The insurgents turn Corinthe's kitchen into one, with mattresses and straw for the badly wounded, and tend the captured municipal guards first.
quote: the kitchen appropriated for the ambulance

text: Charles Jeanne, a worker and former soldier, led the strongest real barricade of June 1832, by the church of Saint-Merry, which held out until the afternoon of the 6th. Hugo quotes his grim answer to the hungry men here, and in the next chapter the insurgents' cry as it was recorded in the trial papers. He sets his invented barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie beside this historical one.
quote: in the barricade Saint-Merry, Jeanne, surrounded by the insurgents

term: Harmodius and Aristogiton, Brutus, Chereas, Stephanus, Charlotte Corday, Sand
text: A roll of political assassins. Harmodius and Aristogiton killed the Athenian tyrant's brother; Brutus killed Caesar; Chaerea killed Caligula; Stephanus killed Domitian; Charlotte Corday killed Marat in his bath in 1793; the student Karl Sand killed the playwright Kotzebue in 1819. Combeferre is thinking of Enjolras's execution of Le Cabuc: each, he says, felt the remorse of having killed.
quote: Harmodius and Aristogiton, Brutus, Chereas, Stephanus, Cromwell, Charlotte Corday, Sand

text: Virgil's poem on farming, which ends its first book with the portents at Caesar's death. Delille's French verse translation (1770) was famous; Malfilâtre, Cournand and Raux made rival versions. That students on a barricade at dawn should argue about them is Hugo's picture of their education and their calm.
quote: comparing the translators of the Georgics

text: Proverbial envious critics: Zoïlus attacked Homer, Maevius Virgil, and Donneau de Visé Molière. Combeferre sets them against Cicero, whose severity towards Caesar he counts as judgement, not envy.
quote: When Zoïlus insults Homer, when Maevius insults Virgil, when Visé insults Molière

text: Latin: “kingly and almost tyrannical”, the verdict of the Roman historian Suetonius on Caesar's conduct after he crossed the Rubicon with his army and made himself master of Rome. Combeferre, a republican, holds that Caesar fell justly.
quote: regia ac pene tyrannica

text: Demes, or villages, of ancient Attica, and the Aeantides were men of the Athenian tribe of Ajax. Bossuet, standing on the paving-stones, shows off a scrap of learning: he wishes he could speak Homer's verse like a native Greek.
quote: Oh Cydathenaeum, Oh Myrrhinus, Oh Probalinthus

term: The fifth of the line and the sixth legion
text: The 5th infantry regiment of the regular army, and the 6th legion of the National Guard. Each of the twelve arrondissements of Paris raised its own legion of citizen guards. Enjolras recognises them by their shakos and standards; the insurgents had hoped some regiment “labored with” by republican agitators would come over to them.
quote: I have picked out the shakos of the fifth of the line, and the standard-bearers of the sixth legion.

text: The blue linen smock was the working man's garment, and in political talk “the blouse” meant the working class, as “the coat” meant the bourgeois. Hugo makes the man who says the barricade's decisive word a nameless worker.
quote: he was some unknown blouse-wearer

text: A military term for a large outpost thrown forward to watch the approaches to a position. Round the barricade every way out leads into one, where a man in a blouse with powder-blackened hands would be shot.
quote: some grand guard of the line or the suburbs

text: Saint-Lazare was the Paris prison and hospital for women, where prostitutes picked up by the police were held. The dead-house is the Morgue, on the island of the Cité, where unidentified bodies were laid out behind glass for families to recognise. Combeferre names the two places the insurgents' women will end up if the breadwinners die.
quote: Misery, prostitution, the police, Saint-Lazare

text: The Hôpital Necker, a charity hospital on the Rue de Sèvres founded by Madame Necker in 1778. A house-surgeon (interne) was a medical student who had won by competition the right to live in and treat patients; Combeferre, the medical student of the group, speaks from what he has seen on its dissecting table.
quote: He was taken to the Necker Hospital, where I saw him. I was house-surgeon in that hospital.

text: Thousands of infants were left each year at the Paris foundling hospital or farmed out to wet-nurses and keepers in the country, and most did not survive childhood. Combeferre's figure of fifty-five percent mortality is, if anything, mild for the period.
quote: the mortality among abandoned children is fifty-five percent

text: Two men of the Revolution, both guillotined in 1794. Saint-Just was Robespierre's young lieutenant, beautiful, pitiless and absolute; Cloots, a Prussian baron who called himself “the orator of the human race”, preached a universal republic of all mankind. Hugo measures Enjolras between the two: too much of the first, not enough of the second.
quote: he had too much of Saint-Just about him, and not enough of Anacharsis Cloots

text: A slip in the translation: Hugo wrote “quatre-vingt-treize”, Ninety-three, the year of the Terror (1793). The “epic and redoubtable school” Enjolras belongs to is that of the men who held that the Republic might use violence to save itself.
quote: “Eighty-three.”

text: The priestess of Apollo at Delphi sat on a bronze tripod over a cleft in the rock and prophesied in a trance. Hugo means that places of death make men prophesy; Enjolras's speech that follows is his oracle.
quote: places where death is have these effects of tripods

term: The hydra, the dragon and the griffin
text: Monsters of ancient myth ruling water, fire and air. Enjolras reads them as the forces man feared and is now taming: the hydra breathing on the waters is the steam locomotive, the griffin of the air is the balloon. The first railways in France were barely a few years old in 1832.
quote: We have vanquished the hydra, and it is called the locomotive

text: The Amphictyonic League was a council of Greek peoples that met twice a year, at Delphi and at Thermopylae, to guard the shrines and settle disputes. Enjolras sees in it the model of a future parliament of Europe and of the world.
quote: The amphictyons had two sittings a year, one at Delphos the seat of the gods, the other at Thermopylae

text: Rousseau's Social Contract (1762) founded the state on an agreement by which each person gives up part of his freedom to the community on equal terms. Enjolras builds his definitions of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity on that idea, and prefers the word “bond”.
quote: Some say social contract

text: Free, compulsory primary schooling: in 1832 a radical demand. The Guizot law of 1833 required every commune to keep a boys' school, but it was neither free for all nor compulsory; France made primary school free and obligatory only in 1881–82. Hugo argued for it all his life.
quote: gratuitous and obligatory instruction

term: A partition of peoples by a congress
text: Enjolras's list of the old world's evils is concrete: wars over royal marriages and successions, and peoples carved up by diplomats, as Poland was partitioned and the map of Europe redrawn at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 without asking the inhabitants.
quote: a partition of peoples by a congress

text: Borrowed from horse harness, where a martingale is the strap from girth to bridle that keeps a horse from tossing its head. In prisons it was a rope from the neck, forking over the stomach and through the legs to the bound hands, so that any struggle tightens it. The insurgents add it to Javert's bonds, with a hobble on his feet “as is done to men on the point of mounting the scaffold”.
quote: that sort of bond which is called in prisons a martingale

term: The avenue of Sphinxes at Thebes
text: The processional road between the temples of Karnak and Luxor in Egypt, lined with hundreds of stone sphinxes. French readers knew it from the engravings of Napoleon's Egyptian expedition. Hugo uses it for the dead silence of the Rue Saint-Denis at dawn.
quote: as dumb as the avenue of Sphinxes at Thebes

term: “Despair, the last weapon … Virgil has said so”
text: Aeneas's line to his comrades on the night Troy falls: “Una salus victis nullam sperare salutem”, the one safety of the defeated is to hope for no safety (Aeneid II). Hugo makes the hopelessness of the barricade its strength.
quote: despair—the last weapon, which sometimes gives victory; Virgil has said so

text: Parts of a field gun's equipment. The fore-carriage (limber) is the two-wheeled front unit that tows the gun and is unhooked to fire; the caisson is the ammunition wagon; the lint-stock (linstock) holds the slow-burning match that is put to the vent to fire the charge. The burning match is what the barricade sees first.
quote: They could see the smoke of the burning lint-stock.

term: A piece of eight and Gribeauval's movable star
text: An eight-pounder, a standard field gun firing an eight-pound ball. Gribeauval reformed French artillery under Louis XV; his “movable star” was a gauge with spring points pushed down the barrel to find flaws in the bore. Combeferre, the scientist, lectures on gun metallurgy while the gun is aimed at him, and ends with the speed of light: “the superiority of Jesus Christ over Napoleon.”
quote: It is a piece of eight, new model, brass

text: A low breastwork thrown up to cover troops or guns from the side. The soldiers make theirs out of the same paving-stones as the barricade, so the street holds two small walls facing each other.
quote: this epaulement

text: Infantry at rest stood their muskets in little pyramids, three or four locked together by the bayonets, ready to be snatched up. A battalion with arms piled is waiting, not attacking, but it closes the street.
quote: A battalion of the line whose arms were piled in the Rue de la Petite Truanderie

text: Parisians in riot quarters stuffed mattresses into their windows against stray bullets, since packed wool or straw stops a musket ball that would go through a shutter. This one hangs from two cords over the poles where the household dried its linen, and the barricade needs it to deaden the grapeshot.
quote: The mattress, placed crosswise, supported at the bottom on two poles for drying linen, was upheld at the top by two ropes

text: The chapter's title recalls what the reader learned of the young tree-pruner of Faverolles: he was a fine shot and something of a poacher, which counted against him at his trial in 1796. The same eye now cuts two cords at the top of a six-storey house.
quote: Jean Valjean took aim at the attic window and fired.

text: Writing in the 1860s, the age of the hooped crinoline skirt and of hair built up over pads and horsehair, Hugo contrasts it with the plain smoothed bands and curls of 1832, when a girl could do her hair in a few minutes.
quote: when women did not swell out their curls and bands with cushions and puffs, and did not put crinoline in their locks

text: House martins, small blue-black and white swallows, build cup-shaped mud nests under cornices and eaves and return to them every spring. Cosette, who cannot see the street, watches the parent birds feeding their brood.
quote: there was a martin’s nest

text: The Paris fire service, the sapeurs-pompiers, was a military corps under the army, wearing brass helmets. That is why a fireman is posted as a lookout on a roof, and why his helmet makes so easy a mark in the sun.
quote: A fireman had placed his back against a tall chimney

term: Pantin des Vertus or la Cunette
text: Places on the edge of Paris beyond the customs wall (Pantin lies in the old plain of the Vertus to the north-east), where wine paid no city duty and Parisians went out on Sundays to drink and dance in guinguettes and tea-gardens. Hugo's example of the suburban National Guard is a dance-hall keeper dying for the order that keeps his trade open.
quote: Pantin des Vertus or la Cunette

text: Lacedaemon is Sparta, byword for patriotic courage. Hugo's irony: the shopkeepers of 1832 defended the shop, “that immense diminutive of the fatherland”, with the spirit of Thermopylae.
quote: with Lacedaemonian enthusiasm

text: Hugo's mock-coinage for the party of order under the July Monarchy: those who backed the government against every disturbance. His point is that the side of order was itself disorderly, with National Guard captains attacking on their own initiative.
quote: governmentalism (the barbarous name of the correct party)

text: Fannicot is the National Guard captain whose company, Hugo says, both shot Jean Prouvaire and threw itself at the barricade without orders; he cites the judicial inquiry of 1832 for it. Henri Fonfrède was a real Bordeaux journalist, a fierce defender of the government with his pen.
quote: some of the sword, like Fannicot, others of the pen, like Henri Fonfrède

text: Summary punishment without trial, named by most accounts after Charles Lynch, a Virginia justice of the American Revolution. Hugo applies it to National Guard platoons that made themselves “a private council of war” and shot prisoners in five minutes, as they shot Prouvaire.
quote: Fierce Lynch law

term: Saint-Simonians and the Duc de Saint-Simon
text: The Saint-Simonians were followers of the social reformer Henri de Saint-Simon, preaching an industrial religion of the poor, and much mocked in 1832. The Duc de Saint-Simon, a different man, wrote famous memoirs of the court of Louis XIV. A National Guard who could not tell them apart nearly killed a poet for carrying the wrong book.
quote: There’s another of those Saint-Simonians!

text: The arcaded square in the Marais built under Henri IV, now the Place des Vosges. No. 6, where the hunted poet takes refuge under the carriage entrance, is the house where Hugo himself lived from 1832 to 1848.
quote: the porte-cochère of No. 6

text: A general's phrase for letting the insurrection exhaust itself before attacking: leave the barricades to burn up their men and cartridges. It is the tactic of the whole morning, which Fannicot's charge spoils.
quote: “the insurrection to fry in its own fat,”

text: The fortress east of Paris that served as the army's great arsenal and artillery depot. Repression “does not count its shots” because it has Vincennes behind it; the barricade has only what is in its cartridge-boxes.
quote: as it has Vincennes, it does not count its shots

term: Quid divinum; the 10th of August and the 29th of July
text: Quid divinum, Latin for “something divine”, is the moment an uprising becomes a revolution. The 10th of August 1792 was the storming of the Tuileries that ended the monarchy; the 29th of July 1830 was the last of the three days that drove out Charles X. Hugo's two examples of a riot that the whole city joined.
quote: a 10th of August is in the air, a 29th of July is in the air

term: Marshal Soult and Suchet at Saragossa
text: Soult, one of Napoleon's marshals, was Louis-Philippe's minister of war in 1832. In the Peninsular War the French took Saragossa in 1809 only after weeks of house-to-house fighting against the whole population; the remark Hugo gives to Marshal Suchet, about old women emptying chamber-pots on the soldiers, is the old campaigner's knowledge that a city is lost once its households join in.
quote: We are lost when the old women empty their pots de chambre on our heads.

text: A short, crowded old street running up from the Pont Notre-Dame towards the Hôtel de Ville, one of the poorest corners of the centre. Pottery thrown from its roofs at the troops was the sign Soult feared: the households joining in.
quote: In the Rue Planche-Mibray, they threw old pieces of pottery

term: The Porte Saint-Martin and the cuirassiers
text: The Porte Saint-Martin is a triumphal arch of Louis XIV on the northern boulevards, a usual place for crowds and trouble. Cuirassiers were heavy cavalry in steel breastplates; the army used them to clear the open boulevards, where barricades could not hold.
quote: In front of the Porte Saint-Martin, a young man, armed with a rifle, attacked alone a squadron of cavalry

text: Françoise d'Aubigné, wife of the poor comic poet Scarron and later, as Madame de Maintenon, the secret wife of Louis XIV. The story went that at her dinners, when there was no roast, a servant whispered “Madame, one more story”, and her wit took the place of the meat.
quote: like Madame Scarron, replaced nourishment with pleasantry

text: In Ariosto's Orlando Furioso the paladin Roland goes mad for love of the princess Angelica. Bossuet's theory is that all heroism comes from women, which makes Enjolras, who loves no one, a puzzle.
quote: Roland gets himself killed for Angélique

text: Latin: the fatherland. It is Enjolras's whole answer to Bossuet's question of whom he loves, and the “mistress” of the chapter's title.
quote: “Patria.”

text: Here the French word for the cartridge-box itself, the leather pouch on a soldier's belt; Hugo uses it beside “cartridge-box” for the same thing. Each dead Guardsman's pouch holds a supply of ready-made cartridges the barricade can no longer make.
quote: emptied the cartridge-box or cartouche as a monkey opens a nut

term: “C’est la faute à Voltaire … c’est la faute à Rousseau”
text: “It’s Voltaire’s fault … it’s Rousseau’s fault.” A satirical refrain of the Restoration, mocking the clergy and royalists who blamed every ill of France on the two philosophers of the Enlightenment. Gavroche improvises new couplets on it under fire (“I am not a notary … I am a little bird … misery is my trousseau”). Nanterre and Palaiseau are just villages near Paris that rhyme.
quote: C’est la faute à Voltaire

text: The giant of Greek myth who drew new strength each time he touched his mother, the Earth; Hercules beat him by holding him in the air. For the street boy, Hugo says, the pavement is his earth.
quote: there was something of Antaeus in that pygmy

text: Gavroche's vocabulary at its most mixed. “Instanter” is lawyer's Latin for “at once”, picked up on the street; “Fichtre!” is a mild French oath, something like “Blimey!”.
quote: “Instanter,” said Gavroche.

term: Barrière d’Enfer and the Esplanade de l’Observatoire
text: The streets just south of the Luxembourg garden: the Rue d’Enfer ran to the Barrière d’Enfer, a toll gate in the customs wall, and the Observatory stood at the end of the long avenue below the garden. Showmen and their booths gathered on such open ground at the edge of the city.
quote: at the Barrière d’Enfer; or on the Esplanade de l’Observatoire

text: Latin from the Christmas gospel: “They found the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes” (Luke 2). It was carved over the door of the Paris foundling hospital in the Rue d’Enfer, where abandoned babies were taken in. Hugo sets the lost boys within sight of it.
quote: Invenerunt parvulum pannis involutum

text: Hugo's examples of “magnificent egoists of the infinite”: the Roman poet of contented retirement; Goethe, the Olympian of Weimar, accused of looking coolly on the suffering of his age; and perhaps La Fontaine, the dreamy fabulist. Great minds, he says, who see the stars and not the hungry child.
quote: Horace was one of them; so was Goethe. La Fontaine perhaps

text: The Roman god of fire and the forge, lame from being thrown out of heaven by Jupiter. Hugo's proof that one may be immortal and still limp.
quote: One may be immortal and yet limp: witness Vulcan.

text: Virgil, Georgics I: “Who would dare to call the sun false?” In Virgil the sun's signs never deceive; Hugo turns the line on the sunlike geniuses he has just criticised, and answers that above the sun there is God.
quote: Solem quis dicere falsum audeat?

text: Trees planted in a repeating pattern of five, four at the corners of a square and one in the middle, so that they form straight alleys from every angle. The formal groves of the Luxembourg were planted so.
quote: The quincunxes and flowerbeds shed forth balm

term: The crows of Marie de Medici
text: The Luxembourg palace and garden were built in the 1610s for Marie de Medici, widow of Henri IV and mother of Louis XIII. Hugo pretends the old crows in the tall trees are hers.
quote: The old crows of Marie de Medici were amorous in the tall trees.

term: The swans' hutch and the great basin
text: The large octagonal pool in front of the Luxembourg palace, with a little wooden house for its swans. It is the same basin where Marius once overheard a bourgeois giving his son advice; Hugo suggests it is the same man.
quote: they kept behind the swans’ hutch

text: The Roman winter festival when slaves were licensed to play masters. For the comfortable bourgeois the insurrection is simply the rabble on holiday, and two ragged children by the basin are “Anarchy entering this garden”.
quote: “It is the Saturnalia.”

text: Web-footed birds, a naturalist's term. The bourgeois uses it of the swans to sound learned while he teaches his son kindness to animals by throwing them the cake.
quote: “Throw it to those palmipeds.”

text: The Tuileries palace was the king's residence; the Luxembourg palace housed the Chamber of Peers, the upper house. Hence the bourgeois's line about the distance between royalty and the peerage. “The younger branch” is the house of Orléans, Louis-Philippe's line, cousins of the deposed elder Bourbons; he fears it is doomed.
quote: From the Tuileries to the Luxembourg, there is but the distance which separates Royalty from the peerage

text: Hugo notes that certain houses on the Rue Madame and the Rue d’Enfer, whose backs gave onto the garden, held keys that let their lodgers in after the gates were shut. The well-off can enter when the gates are closed; the poor children are there only by accident.
quote: had keys to the Luxembourg garden

text: The chapter's Latin title: “The dead father awaits the son who is about to die.” It closes on Marius wondering what his dead father, Colonel Pontmercy, will say to him when they meet.
quote: Marius was disturbed with regard to what his father was about to say to him.

text: Hugo's name for a sombre deity of the Spartans, to whom Enjolras is compared “sacrificing his naked sword”. The Epidotes were obscure gods of Sparta; the learned allusion sets Enjolras among the austere heroes of Lacedaemon.
quote: the sombre genius, Epidotas

text: A set of little open shelves for displaying knick-knacks and curios, a “whatnot”, named after the port of Dunkirk, through which such trinkets came. Courfeyrac lays out his sword-cane, gun, pistols and cudgel with the same fond care.
quote: a young girl setting a small dunkerque in order

text: Engineer troops, armed with axes, whose work was to cut through obstacles; they led an assault column to break open the barricade for the infantry behind. Their appearance tells Enjolras the final attack is coming.
quote: A squad of sappers and miners, axe on shoulder

text: The Marquis de Clermont-Tonnerre was Louis XVIII's minister of war from 1823 (minister of the navy in 1822). Hugo credits him with the phrase for the moment when the fighting comes to grips.
quote: M. Clermont-Tonnerre, in 1822, called “the tug of war.”

text: A folding pocket knife, the ordinary tool of a working man or a convict. Javert reads it as fitting: a convict's revenge should be done with a convict's knife.
quote: “A clasp-knife!” exclaimed Javert, “you are right. That suits you better.”

term: A charter granted or a legal country
text: The Charter was the constitution “granted” by Louis XVIII in 1814 and revised in 1830. The “legal country” (pays légal) was the tiny electorate of men rich enough to pay the tax that qualified them to vote, some two hundred thousand in a nation of thirty-two million. Hugo's phrase names a regime of law that left the people outside.
quote: with a charter granted or with a legal country

text: A paradox from the Revolution (les modérés enragés): frightened men of order can turn more savage than radicals. Hugo uses it for the householders behind their shutters, whose fear hardens into hatred of the men dying outside.
quote: “The enraged moderates.”

text: Two names of one goddess: Minerva as the Roman goddess of wisdom, Pallas Athena as the armed warrior with spear and helmet. Utopia turns into revolution when thought takes up arms.
quote: from Minerva turns to Pallas

text: Romantic poet and friend of Hugo's youth, who hanged himself in 1855. His remark “God is dead, perhaps” reads, Hugo says, as despair at a halt in progress.
quote: “God is dead, perhaps,” said Gerard de Nerval

term: John Brown and Washington; Pisacane and Garibaldi
text: Hugo's pairs of the failed martyr and the successful hero. John Brown raided Harper's Ferry in 1859 to start a slave rising and was hanged; Hugo had pleaded publicly for his life. Carlo Pisacane landed in southern Italy in 1857 to raise revolt and was killed; Garibaldi succeeded in 1860. These are events of Hugo's exile, years after 1832.
quote: John Brown is greater than Washington, and Pisacane is greater than Garibaldi.

term: Pavements of hell and the bear's paving-stone
text: Two proverbs. The road to hell is paved with good intentions, so the barricade is “made of good intentions”. In La Fontaine's fable the bear, meaning to kill a fly on his sleeping friend's face, crushes his head with a paving-stone; “the bear's paving-stone” (le pavé de l'ours) is a kindness that kills.
quote: when we behold the pavement, we think of the bear

text: In secret ballots, clubs and juries voted with white balls for yes and black for no. An insurrection, Hugo says, is an idea passing its examination before the people; if they drop in a black ball, it is only a riot.
quote: If the people lets fall a black ball

text: Leonidas led the three hundred Spartans who died holding the pass of Thermopylae against the Persians; Don Quixote is Cervantes's knight who tilts at windmills. The insurgents, Hugo says, think of the first and not of the second.
quote: We do not think of Don Quixote but of Leonidas.

text: From Lucretius: “they hand on the torch of life”, like runners in a torch race. Hugo's torch of civilisation passes from Greece to Italy to France. (The text runs the words together.)
quote: Vitaelampada tradunt

text: Corinth was the rich and artistic Greek city; Sybaris in southern Italy was so luxurious that “sybarite” came to mean a pampered voluptuary. A civilising people should be artistic, Hugo says, but not soft.
quote: Corinth, yes; Sybaris, no.

term: A Missouri or a South Carolina
text: Two American slave states, writing in the early 1860s as the Civil War began. When France falls into materialism, Hugo says, her ideas shrink to the size of slaveholders' politics.
quote: of the dimensions of a Missouri or a South Carolina

text: The philosopher who died for the truth, set against Shakespeare's fat, cowardly, witty knight who lives for sack and comfort. A nation that “bites the mire and finds it good” has traded the one for the other.
quote: it has abandoned Socrates for Falstaff

text: Light infantry raised in Algeria from 1830, at first from Kabyle tribesmen and later from Frenchmen in their Arab-style dress, famous for dash in the attack. Hugo's phrase means the citizen-soldiers of 1832 fought like crack colonial troops.
quote: a National Guardsman fought like a Zouave

text: The republicans of 1832 had counted on officers of the old imperial army, friends of the dead General Lamarque, to bring troops over to them. None came. Hugo leaves Feuilly's “celebrated names” in brackets, unsaid.
quote: who are our generals, and who abandon us

text: The long quotation is a battle catalogue from the Iliad (Book VI), where each Greek hero kills a named Trojan with a line of family history. Hugo sets it beside the medieval romances (Esplandian, a hero of the Amadis cycle, against the giant Swantibore) and the painted dukes of Brittany and Bourbon, then insists that a raw recruit and a medical student killing each other in a Paris alley are as great as any of them.
quote: Diomedes cuts the throat of Axylus

text: At Marignano in 1515 the young King François I fought all day against the Swiss pikemen, and legend had him break three swords, or end with stumps of them in his hands. Enjolras ends with four.
quote: one more than François I at Marignan

text: One of the hells of Hindu scripture, Asipatravana, where the damned are cut by trees whose leaves are blades. Hugo's comparison for the hand-to-hand fighting on the barricade.
quote: the Forest of Swords

text: Two humble spots of old Paris: a crossroads in the Marais and a narrow street by the Seine near the Hôtel de Ville. Hugo's point is that any ordinary corner of the city can become an epic battlefield.
quote: the Carrefour Boucherat or in the blind alley Planche-Mibray

text: A defensive move in singlestick or quarterstaff fencing, whirling the stick round the head to make a guard on every side. Enjolras uses his rifle like a stick to beat back the bayonets as he covers the door.
quote: what singlestick players call a “covered rose” round his head

text: In April 1834, during another republican rising, soldiers who believed a shot had come from No. 12 Rue Transnonain broke in and killed the inhabitants, men, women and children. Daumier's lithograph of the scene made it a byword for army reprisal. Hugo names it as the sort of massacre such rumours produce.
quote: the catastrophe of the Rue Transnonain

text: José de Palafox, defender of Saragossa against the French in 1808. Summoned to surrender, he is said to have replied “War to the knife.” The wine-shop, Hugo says, fought like a house of Saragossa, room by room.
quote: “After the war with cannon, the war with knives.”

text: Latin for “strong water”: nitric acid, used by engravers and metalworkers. These are the fifteen sealed bottles from the cellar that Enjolras kept back. Thrown down the stairwell they burn and blind; Hugo pleads that the besieged turn everything into a weapon.
quote: They were bottles of aquafortis.

term: Greek fire and Bayard's boiling pitch
text: Greek fire was the Byzantine incendiary that burned even on water (Hugo links it loosely with Archimedes, who defended Syracuse with war-machines); the Chevalier Bayard, the “knight without fear and without reproach”, was the model of chivalry and a famous defender of besieged towns. Neither, Hugo says, was dishonoured by using terrible means.
quote: Greek fire did not disgrace Archimedes, boiling pitch did not disgrace Bayard

term: “Do you wish to have your eyes bandaged?”
text: The courtesy of the firing squad: a condemned man was offered a blindfold, and refusing it was a mark of courage. The officer's question turns a massacre for a moment into an execution.
quote: Do you wish to have your eyes bandaged?

term: “There was an insurgent whom I heard called Apollo”
text: Apollo is the beautiful young god of light. Hugo says such words were spoken before the council of war that tried the insurgents of 1832, and lets the reader decide that they meant Enjolras.
quote: There was an insurgent whom I heard called Apollo.

text: An iron grille about two feet square, set flat in the pavement over a shaft to the drain below, of the kind that let street water run down into the sewers. With the paving torn up for the barricade it lies loose. The fugitive's old “art of escape” sees in it the one way out that is neither over the barricade nor through the soldiers.
quote: an iron grating, placed flat and on a level with the soil

text: Twenty-five million francs a year: Hugo's estimate of what the manure of Paris would be worth as fertiliser if it went to the fields instead of the Seine. For scale, a labourer earned perhaps five or six hundred francs a year; the half-milliard he gives for all France is five hundred million, which he says would pay a quarter of the national budget.
quote: Paris casts twenty-five millions yearly into the water.

text: Seabird droppings accumulated over centuries on rainless islands, above all off Peru, and shipped to Europe in huge quantities from the 1840s as the wonder fertiliser of the age. Hugo's point is the absurdity of sending fleets across the world for bird dung while pouring the city's own into the sea.
quote: There is no guano comparable in fertility with the detritus of a capital.

text: Justus von Liebig, the German chemist who founded agricultural chemistry and argued that a civilisation which does not return its waste to the soil exhausts it. Hugo borrows his claim that the sewers of Rome swallowed the prosperity of the Roman peasant.
quote: “The sewers of Rome,” says Liebig

text: Written in the years of the “Great Stink” of 1858, when the Thames, full of London's sewage, smelled so foul that Parliament could hardly sit; cholera had killed tens of thousands. Hugo, in exile in the Channel Islands, followed the English drainage debates closely.
quote: the Thames is poisoning London

text: Below Paris, at Saint-Cloud, nets were stretched across the Seine, and it was there that the bodies of the drowned were caught and recovered. Hugo's grim joke: the public fortune floats away the same road.
quote: There should be nets at Saint-Cloud for the public fortune.

text: Nicolas Beaujon, the immensely rich financier of Louis XV's day, spent fortunes on a pleasure-house and gardens west of Paris, the Folie Beaujon. Here a byword for lavish waste.
quote: its Beaujon folly

text: Lutetia was the Roman name of Paris, usually derived from the Latin lutum, mud, because the first town stood among the marshes of the Seine. Hugo sets it beside the Athens, Tyre and Sparta that Paris also contains.
quote: it also contains Lutetia, the city of mud

text: Three great minds with stained characters: the Florentine theorist of ruthless politics; Francis Bacon, philosopher and Lord Chancellor convicted of taking bribes; Mirabeau, orator of 1789, debauched and secretly in the king's pay. Hugo's phrase for them, “grandiose vileness”, is also his phrase for the sewer.
quote: Macchiavelli, Bacon and Mirabeau, grandiose vileness

text: A reef-building coral, honeycombed with channels. Hugo's image for the ground under Paris: riddled with the catacombs (the old quarries where the bones of emptied cemeteries were stacked), gas pipes, water mains feeding the street fountains, and the sewers.
quote: a colossal madrepore

text: The great sewer that ran in an arc along the right bank, following the line of an old stream bed round the north of the old city, into which the smaller drains of the right bank emptied. It is the trunk of Hugo's “branch grafted on the river”.
quote: the belt sewer will form the trunk of this branch

text: Two false prophets with stage effects. John of Leyden ruled the Anabaptist kingdom of Münster in 1534–35 and was executed; Mokanna, the veiled prophet of Khorasan in the eighth century, was said to make a false moon rise from a well. (Hugo swaps their tricks.) Moore's poem Lalla Rookh made Mokanna famous.
quote: Mokanna, the veiled prophet of Khorassan

text: The Gemonian Stairs in Rome, where the bodies of executed criminals were thrown and left before being dragged to the Tiber. Hugo treats them as Rome's sewer; the point is that the city's refuse tells its history.
quote: The Germoniae narrated Rome.

term: Maillotins, tire-laine, Huguenots, Morin's illuminated, chauffeurs
text: Hugo's procession of those who hid underground, one for each century. The Maillotins were Paris rioters of 1382 armed with lead mallets; the tire-laine (“cloak-snatchers”) were night thieves; the Huguenots, persecuted Protestants; Simon Morin, a visionary burned for heresy in 1663, and his followers; the chauffeurs, bandits of the 1790s who roasted their victims' feet to make them reveal their money.
quote: the maillotins in the fourteenth century, the tire-laine of the fifteenth

text: The beggars' enclaves of old Paris, where cripples and blind men were “miraculously” cured each night when they came home from begging. Hugo had made the most famous of them a setting in Notre-Dame de Paris; here the sewer is its annexe.
quote: the adjunct of the Cour des Miracles

text: Real old street names of Paris: Vide-Gousset means “Empty-Purse”, Coupe-Gorge “Cut-Throat”. The thieves who worked them by day slept in the drains by night.
quote: the blind-alley Vide-Gousset, or the Rue Coupe-Gorge

text: François Villon, the fifteenth-century poet who was a thief and nearly hanged, and Rabelais, the sixteenth-century comic genius of gross humour. Through the sewer's air-holes the underworld poet talks with the laughing one above.
quote: Villon within converses with Rabelais without

term: The mask of Basil and Scapin's false nose
text: Stage hypocrites: Basile is the slandering music-master of Beaumarchais's Barber of Seville, Scapin the scheming valet of Molière's comedy. In the sewer their masks show the cardboard and strings: everything there is what it really is.
quote: The mask of Basil is to be found there

term: Historic murderers sponging out their work
text: Hugo's roll of royal and revolutionary killers and their instruments: Louis XI and his executioner-provost Tristan; François I and his chancellor Duprat; Charles IX and his mother Catherine de Medici, authors of the Saint Bartholomew massacre of Protestants in 1572; Richelieu and Louis XIII; Louvois and Le Tellier, ministers of Louis XIV's persecutions; Hébert and Maillard of the Terror.
quote: Louis XI is there with Tristan

text: Wife of the Emperor Claudius, notorious in Roman satire for slipping out at night to a brothel. Philosophy, Hugo says, can read even her elbow-mark on the cloaks of Rome's porters.
quote: the mark of Messalina’s elbowing

text: Louis-Sébastien Mercier, whose Tableau de Paris (1781–88) described the city street by street, its dirt included. Hugo cites him as his witness that the sewer was then left to itself.
quote: Mercier attests the fact

text: Daedalus built the Labyrinth of Crete; Babel is the tower of confused tongues. Old Paris was Babel above, its streets and authorities unintelligible, and a labyrinth below.
quote: Daedalus backed up Babel

text: When the Seine rose in 1802 it drove back up the sewers and the filth burst out into the streets, over the Place des Victoires with its statue of Louis XIV and across both banks. Hugo's street-by-street list and measurements read like an official report, which is the effect he wants.
quote: The inundation of 1802

term: Sainte-Foix and the Marquis de Créqui
text: An eighteenth-century anecdote: Saint-Foix, a playwright famous for his quarrels and duels, and the great nobleman Créqui hobnobbing atop a scavenger's cart. Hugo uses it to recall that in that age the carts of street refuse emptied straight into the sewer mouths.
quote: Sainte-Foix fraternized with the Marquis de Créqui

text: The Paris nickname for the sewer, in French the Trou Punais, “the stinking hole”; the English renders it after the polyp, a word also used of a foul growth in the nose. Rome had dignified its refuse with a name; Paris insulted its own.
quote: Paris insulted hers, and entitled it the Polypus-Hole

text: Legends of the sewer. The Marmousets were the low-born counsellors of Charles VI, overthrown in 1392; Hugo repeats the tale that their corpses were thrown into a drain. Fagon, Louis XIV's physician, blamed a deadly fever of 1685 on the open sewer of the Marais, a mouth in the Rue Saint-Louis that stayed open until 1833.
quote: the corpses of the Marmousets had been cast into the sewer de la Barillerie

text: Hugo's deliberately offhand naming of Napoleon's minister: Crétet was Minister of the Interior from 1807, Decrès Minister of the Navy. The vagueness puts the great man in his place beside the sewerman.
quote: some Decrès or Crétet or other

text: A roll-call of the armies of the Republic and the Empire before Austerlitz (December 1805): the generals Hoche, Kléber, Desaix and Marceau; the balloonists who observed at Fleurus in 1794; the bridge of Lodi and siege of Mantua in the Italian campaign; the French cavalry that captured the Dutch fleet frozen in the ice in 1795. Hugo heaps up glory in order to set Bruneseau above it.
quote: the aérostiers of Fleurus

text: Pierre-Emmanuel Bruneseau, inspector of sanitation under Napoleon, who between 1805 and 1812 led the first systematic survey of the Paris sewers, mapping and cleaning galleries no one had entered for generations. Hugo makes him an explorer of the underworld, the Columbus of the cesspool.
quote: This man existed and his name was Bruneseau.

text: Antoine-François Fourcroy, the chemist and colleague of Lavoisier, a public-health adviser under Napoleon. His remedy for the sewer's poisonous air was fire: cages of resin-soaked tow burned to purify the galleries.
quote: On the advice of Fourcroy

text: The great Renaissance architect of Henri II and Catherine de Medici, builder of the Tuileries. Bruneseau found a stone dated 1550 marking how far Delorme's inspection of the drains had gone: the high-water mark of the sixteenth century.
quote: Philibert Delorme, charged by Henri II with visiting the subterranean drains of Paris

text: A stream that once ran from the heights of Ménilmontant round the north of old Paris to the Seine. From 1412 it was walled and made the Grand Sewer, the belt sewer of the right bank: a country brook promoted to royal service, as if a peasant (Gros-Jean) became Lebel, Louis XV's first valet.
quote: something like Gros-Jean transformed into Lebel

term: The orang-utan and the devil of the Rue des Bernardins
text: Among Bruneseau's finds, the skeleton of an ape escaped from the Jardin des Plantes zoo in 1800. Hugo connects it, straight-faced, with a famous sighting of “the devil” in a nearby street that year.
quote: the skeleton of an orangutan, who had disappeared from the Jardin des Plantes in 1800

text: An old vaulted outfall of the sewer on the Seine, near the Quai de la Mégisserie on the right bank, where a long drain ended. It gave its name to the spot; the sewermen's finds there (here, a ragpicker's basket preserved whole) were the stuff of legend.
quote: this long, arched drain which terminated at the Arche-Marion

text: Protestant satire of the Wars of Religion: a copper medal showing a pig in a cardinal's hat and a wolf wearing the papal tiara, mocking the Catholic hierarchy as greedy and predatory. Owning one could be dangerous; someone dropped it down a drain.
quote: the pig hooded with a cardinal’s hat

text: Jean-Paul Marat, “the Friend of the People”, the most violent journalist of the Revolution, was stabbed in his bath in 1793. Before the Revolution he had been a physician in the household of the Comte d'Artois. His body was placed in the Panthéon in 1794 and thrown out a few months later. Hugo's story of the embroidered sheet from a marquise (LAVBESP, Laubespine) carries him from the bed of a great lady to the rats.
quote: a morsel of the shroud of Marat

text: A very fine, soft linen or cotton cloth, used for handkerchiefs, shirts and the best bed-linen, named after a legendary weaver of Cambrai. A scrap of it on a hinge in the sewer was an aristocratic object in the wrong place.
quote: It was of very fine batiste

text: Watteau painted the silks and amorous parties of the early eighteenth century; Dante descended into Hell. The rag of Marat's shroud begins as the one and ends as the other.
quote: This chamber rag, of which Watteau would formerly have joyfully sketched every fold

text: Hugo uses the English word in quotation marks: to a French ear it summed up English propriety. The modern sewer is like a tradesman made councillor of state (a member of the Conseil d'État, the government's highest administrative body): risen, clean and dull.
quote: what is understood in England by the word “respectable.”

term: The rectilinear alexandrine and the Rue de Rivoli
text: The alexandrine, the twelve-syllable line of French classical tragedy, which the Romantics (Hugo first among them) broke up; the Rue de Rivoli, Napoleon's long straight arcaded street. The new sewer is as regular as both: classicism banished from poetry has gone underground.
quote: the classical rectilinear alexandrine

text: Molière's Tartuffe is the religious hypocrite who wears piety as a mask. The clean modern sewer, Hugo says, still gives off a suspicious smell like him fresh from confession: more hypocritical than irreproachable.
quote: like Tartuffe after confession

text: The filthiest place in Greek myth: King Augeas's stables, uncleaned for thirty years, which Hercules washed out in a day by turning two rivers through them. Even Tartuffe's conscience is an improvement on them.
quote: Tartuffe’s conscience is a progress over the Augean stables

text: Hugo's figures, reign by reign, show the network growing from about twenty-three kilometres under the old monarchy to some two hundred and twenty-six by the early 1860s, ten times over, most of it built under Louis-Philippe and then Napoleon III (“the present government”) as Haussmann rebuilt Paris. A league is about four kilometres.
quote: sixty leagues of sewers

text: French for “mustards”: the sewer-diggers' name for the soft, yellowish, liquid clays under Paris that swallowed tools and men. One of several hazards of a soil Hugo calls “rebellious to the pick”.
quote: which special science calls moutardes

text: Two waters of Paris. The Bièvre, a small river of the Left Bank fouled by tanneries and dye-works, was vaulted over and turned into a sewer. The Ourcq canal, dug under Napoleon, brought drinking water to the city from the north-east.
quote: vaulted the Bièvre from the Boulevard de l’Hôpital, as far as the Seine

text: A works superintendent and an engineer of the Paris sewers who, Hugo says, died of the work, after cutting galleries through quicksand and putrid ground. He names them as soldiers of a war that issues no bulletins.
quote: Duleau the engineer died

text: The cholera epidemic of spring 1832 killed some eighteen thousand Parisians. Only fear of it, Hugo says, produced the rebuilding of the sewers that Bruneseau had begun; as late as 1821 a stretch of the belt sewer still lay open to the sky like a canal.
quote: the cholera was required to bring about the vast reconstruction

text: The road engineers' name for the big barred gratings at the bottom of a sunken street, where gutters met, worn slippery by feet and dangerous to horses. Many Paris streets of 1832 dipped in the middle to drain into them, instead of rising in the middle as they later did.
quote: the expressive name of Cassis

text: An artesian well bored at Grenelle, on the Left Bank, between 1833 and 1841, more than five hundred metres down to the water-bearing sands beneath Paris. Its water was thought to gather the rivers of half of France, which is Hugo's “one drinks the Seine … and the Loire in a glass”.
quote: the well of Grenelle

text: The sewerman's trade was as despised and feared as the knacker's (the man who slaughtered worn-out horses and rendered carcasses), long left to the executioner's family. High wages were needed to get men down, and the proverb said that to go into the sewer was to enter the grave.
quote: to descend into the sewer is to enter the grave

text: Every Paris sewer runs downhill to the Seine, so the slope underfoot is the thread through the labyrinth: follow the water and you reach the river. That is exactly why Valjean climbs against it, since the nearest outlets would put him in daylight at the busiest spot in the city.
quote: To follow to the slope is to arrive at the river.

term: Between the Pont au Change and the Pont-Neuf
text: The stretch of right-bank quay facing the Île de la Cité, at the heart of Paris, crowded with traffic, markets and guard posts. An outlet there was the worst place to come up with a bleeding insurgent on one's back.
quote: between the Pont au Change and the Pont-Neuf

text: The sewermen's word for a blind side-passage that leads nowhere. Valjean has landed in one, walled behind him, with only the faint light from the shaft he came down.
quote: one of those blind alleys, which the special jargon terms branches

term: The Post-Office and the rotunda of the Wheat Market
text: Landmarks above the sewers west of the Halles: the central Post-Office in the Rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau and the round domed Halle au Blé, the grain exchange. Hugo names the streets above each gallery so that the reader can follow the route on a map, while Valjean cannot.
quote: under the Post-Office and under the rotunda of the Wheat Market

term: Eight hundred livres the fathom; petits matériaux
text: Two scales of cost and quality. The royal sewer under the Rue Saint-Denis was granite and mortar at eight hundred livres the fathom (toise, about two metres); the new work of Valjean's gallery was porous stone and concrete at two hundred francs the metre, in “small stuff”, cheap bourgeois masonry. Hugo slips a social comparison into the stonework.
quote: the bourgeoise masonry known as à petits matériaux

term: “Like the prophet, he was in the belly of the monster”
text: Jonah, swallowed by the great fish and kept three days in its belly before being cast up alive. The image fits the book's title for this section, the intestine of Paris.
quote: Like the prophet, he was in the belly of the monster.

term: The watershed of the right bank
text: A low ridge under the right bank divides the drainage: one side runs straight down to the Seine, the other north into the Grand Sewer, which carries its water round to come out far downstream. When the water starts running with him, Valjean has crossed the crest.
quote: The ridge which the soil of Paris forms on its right bank empties one of its watersheds into the Seine and the other into the Grand Sewer.

text: A hunting term: beaters drive game out of cover towards the guns. On 6 June the police beat the sewers for fugitive insurgents while the army swept the streets.
quote: a battue of the sewers had been ordered

text: Henri Gisquet was Prefect of Police of Paris in 1832, the official whose signature was on Javert's card. Thomas Bugeaud, a general of the July Monarchy and later the conqueror of Algeria, is Hugo's commander for the troops in the streets. One searches “occult Paris”, the other “public Paris”.
quote: Prefect Gisquet was to search occult Paris while General Bugeaud swept public Paris

text: Slang of the early 1830s for a young republican hothead, from the glazed sailor's hat (bousingot) such youths affected. Hugo notes it filled the gap between “Jacobin”, gone stale, and “demagogue”, which came later.
quote: any “bousingot” to track out

text: Police slang, from the French filer, to tail a suspect without arresting him, in the hope that he will lead the way to his accomplices. The agent in this chapter does it by the book, with a hackney-coach following on the quay above in case it is needed.
quote: This delicate operation is called “spinning.”

term: Blue and red: clothed by the state
text: Hugo's sour joke on two uniforms the state hands out. The agent wears blue, the colour of soldiers and officials; the galley convict wore a red jacket. “There is a purple from below”: the red of the prison is the dark twin of royal purple.
quote: To be dressed in blue is glorious; to be dressed in red is disagreeable.

text: Hugo quotes the secret instructions of the Paris police: “Always have on hand a hackney-coach.” Fiacres plied for hire everywhere, and drivers knew the agents; one signal and the empty coach turns and keeps pace above the quay.
quote: “Always have on hand a hackney-coach, in case of emergency.”

term: The watering slope and the shore below the quay
text: In 1832 the right bank below the Champs-Élysées, between the Pont des Invalides and the Pont de Jéna, was still a strip of open shore under the quay wall, with a ramp down which cab-drivers coming from Passy brought their horses to drink. The later embankments did away with both, as Hugo complains.
quote: permitted cabdrivers arriving from Passy to come to the river and water their horses

text: A Renaissance house front taken down at Moret-sur-Loing and rebuilt on the Cours-la-Reine in 1824 by Colonel Brack, as a fashionable antique. Hugo uses it as a landmark for the deserted stretch of shore.
quote: the house brought to Paris from Moret in 1824, by Colonel Brack

text: The river outlets of the sewers were closed with locked iron gratings, and only the authorities held keys. The pursuer's outrage is that the man has not picked the lock with a hook but opened it with an official key, which he should not have.
quote: “That is too much! A government key!”

text: The canvas bag of oats strapped over a cab-horse's muzzle while it waits. Hugo's parenthesis that the Government sometimes applies it to Parisians means it muzzles them with a ration.
quote: encased his horses’ muzzles in the bag of oats

text: The old walled brook of Ménilmontant, the main collector of the right bank: eight feet wide and seven high, about two leagues long, curving round the north of the city to its outlet far downstream. Despite the name “belt”, Hugo stresses, it is not a ring: upstream it ends in a dead end at the foot of Ménilmontant, so turning left, downstream, was the only right choice.
quote: The Grand Sewer is, in fact, eight feet wide and seven feet high.

text: The raised ledge or footway running along the side of a sewer gallery above the channel of running water. Valjean lays Marius on it under the light of an air-hole to bind his wounds.
quote: deposited Marius on the banquette of the sewer

term: The Isle Louviers and the Arsenal
text: At the eastern end of old Paris, near the Bastille: the Île Louviers was a small island of timber-yards in the Seine, joined to the right bank in 1843, and the Arsenal was the old royal powder and artillery works beside it. Hugo traces the route through the sewers by which Valjean might have reached an outlet there, and which he could not have known.
quote: above the ancient Isle Louviers

text: The sewermen's word for a spot where water had seeped under the floor of a gallery and turned the subsoil to liquid mud, so that the pavement sagged or gave way into a slough. It might be three feet deep or bottomless, solid enough to hold a child or loose enough to swallow a man in minutes. Hugo calls it “the beach of Mont Saint-Michel in a sewer”, and says such slips were common before the rebuilding begun in 1833.
quote: was called a fontis, in the special tongue

term: Quicksands of Brittany and Mont Saint-Michel
text: The bay round Mont Saint-Michel, between Normandy and Brittany, has vast tidal flats where the sea retreats for miles and the sand, soaked from beneath, can liquefy under a walker's feet. Pilgrims and fishermen drowned there, and the danger was notorious. Hugo knew such coasts from his years in the Channel Islands.
quote: it is the beach of Mont Saint-Michel in a sewer

text: A sticky paste smeared on twigs to trap small birds by the feet. The wet sand of the quicksand holds the walker the same way.
quote: it is no longer sand, it is birdlime

term: Clarence and the butt of Malvoisie
text: George, Duke of Clarence, brother of Edward IV, was put to death in the Tower in 1478 and, by tradition, drowned in a cask of Malmsey (Malvoisie), a sweet Greek wine; Shakespeare uses the story in Richard III. Hugo grants that death a certain dignity, against death in a scavenger's ditch.
quote: To die in a butt of Malvoisie, like Clarence, is permissible

term: Escoubleau and the Duchesse de Sourdis
text: Hugo's tale of a young officer of the house of Escoubleau, surprised with his cousin the Duchesse de Sourdis, who hid in a drain to escape the duke and drowned in its mire. At the siege of Lérida in Catalonia (1647) Condé's officers were said to have gone to the assault in silk stockings with violins playing; the dandy hero dies a dandy's opposite.
quote: Vicomte d’Escoubleau

text: The Cemetery of the Holy Innocents beside the Halles, for centuries the great common burial ground of Paris, with its charnel-house galleries of bones. It was closed in 1780 as a danger to health and emptied into the catacombs in 1785–87; the market and the Fountain of the Innocents took its place.
quote: the cemetery called the Charnier des Innocents, in 1785

text: A street in the north-east of Paris whose name means Shrovetide, the days of feasting before Lent. Its manhole is where the sewerman Blaise Poutrain was swallowed in a fontis.
quote: the manhole of the Rue Carême-Prenant

text: Read Panthéon: the huge domed church of Sainte-Geneviève on the Left Bank hill, built from 1758 and made a temple for great men in 1791. Its weight crushed old underground vaults beneath it. The English edition misprints the name.
quote: the heaping up of the Parthenon

term: Hero and Leander; Pyramus and Thisbe
text: Two pairs of lovers from Greek and Roman legend whose love outlasts death: Hero mourned Leander drowned swimming the Hellespont to her, and Thisbe killed herself over Pyramus's body. In the sewer, Hugo says, love does not hold: Hero will not wash the body, Thisbe holds her nose.
quote: Hero refuses to wash the body of Leander.

text: Hydrogen sulphide, the rotten-egg gas given off by sewage, poisonous in quantity. It was the sewermen's great danger before ventilation, and its stench is what Hugo sets in place of a sea wind.
quote: sulfuretted hydrogen in place of the hurricane

text: The western end of the right bank, towards the Seine, lies on loose river sand, as do the Saint-Georges and Martyrs quarters to the north on their gassy clay. Rebuilding the sewer under the Faubourg Saint-Honoré in 1836 took six months for that reason. It tells the reader where Valjean now is: under the rich new west of Paris, of mansions (hôtels) and carriages.
quote: the quicksand, which forms the subsoil of the Champs-Élysées as far as the Seine

text: Scenes of Noah's Flood were a favourite subject of painters, from Poussin's Winter to Girodet's Scene of a Deluge (1806), and often showed a figure in the rising water lifting a child above it. Hugo gives Valjean that pose.
quote: In the old paintings of the deluge there is a mother holding her child thus.

text: The valley outside Jerusalem where refuse burned, which became a Jewish and Christian name for hell. Hugo's damned soul sees its way out: daylight at the end of the gallery.
quote: the outlet of Gehenna

text: The sewer's mouth on the right bank between the Pont de Jéna downstream and the Pont des Invalides upstream, looking across the Seine to the Gros-Caillou, the quarter by the Champ de Mars. In 1832 this was the empty western edge of the city, “one of the most solitary points in Paris”. The text spells it “Grand-Caillou”.
quote: the shore which faces the Grand-Caillou

text: The gallery narrows and lowers towards its grating like the wicket of a prison, a design copied, Hugo says, from penitentiaries and later corrected. The double-locked grating with its rusty bolt is exactly what the convict knows best.
quote: imitated from the wickets of penitentiaries

text: Thieves' bargain: split the take. The man with the key assumes he is dealing with a murderer who has robbed his victim, and offers the exit for half the money, a rope and a stone to sink the body thrown in.
quote: “Half shares.”

text: Hugo points to Pierre Corneille, “the elder”, whose tragedies use stupide in its old sense: struck dumb, stunned motionless with astonishment, not foolish.
quote: “remained stupid”—the expression belongs to the elder Corneille

term: The quarter of an hour before the examining magistrate
text: The juge d'instruction questioned suspects in private, with no lawyer present, before any trial; for a criminal it was the dangerous moment, where one careless word could hang him. Silence, Thénardier says approvingly, is good practice for it.
quote: that cursed quarter of an hour before the examining magistrate

text: All Valjean has in his fob: one louis d'or (twenty francs), two five-franc pieces and a few big copper sous. About two weeks' wages for a labourer, and a joke as the price of a murder: “You cut folks’ throats too cheap altogether.”
quote: one louis d’or, two five-franc pieces, and five or six large sous

term: “It’s like the fair, you pay when you go out”
text: At the fairground booths and shows of Paris one sometimes paid not at the door but on leaving. Thénardier's joke turns the sewer into a sideshow and himself into its showman.
quote: It’s like the fair here, you pay when you go out.

text: A short weighted club, the casse-tête (“head-breaker”), carried by plain-clothes agents of the police as a concealed weapon; the lead in its knob made it deadly. It identifies the tall figure before he speaks.
quote: a bludgeon of which the leaden head was visible

text: Old Marais houses opened onto the street by a great carriage gate (porte-cochère) with a heavy knocker; the porter in his lodge inside let visitors in. This one, wrought with a goat and a satyr, belongs to the old style of the eighteenth century, like its owner.
quote: raising the heavy knocker of beaten iron, embellished in the old style

text: Tall cupboards for household linen, the pride of a French household. Nicolette opens them to find sheets and cloth for bandages.
quote: Nicolette opened the linen-presses

text: In Paris apartment houses the front door was opened at night by the porter, who pulled a cord from his bed in the lodge to lift the latch; the visitor called out his name as he passed. “Cordon, s'il vous plaît!” was the nightly formula.
quote: called to the porter who was in bed and who had pulled the cord from his couch

text: A napoleon was the gold twenty-franc coin, so four make the eighty francs the coachman asks for seven hours and his ruined velvet cushions. It is a large sum, and Javert pays it from his own pocket at once, without the official certificate the man asks him to sign.
quote: Javert drew four napoleons from his pocket

term: The posts of the Blancs-Manteaux and the Archives
text: Guard posts near the Rue de l’Homme Armé, named after the Blancs-Manteaux, the old monastery and street of the “White Cloaks” friars, and after the Archives at the end of the street. Valjean assumes Javert will lock him up in one of them.
quote: the post of the Blancs-Manteaux or to the post of the Archives

text: The Stations of the Cross, the fourteen halts of Christ's road to Calvary, at which the faithful pause in prayer. Valjean's pause on the first-floor landing is one.
quote: All sorrowful roads have their stations.

text: Loose sheets of raw cotton, used for padding clothes. With no lint in the house, the doctor packs Marius's wounds with it to stop the bleeding, while Basque and Nicolette tear the household linen into bandages.
quote: the doctor, for the time being, arrested the bleeding with layers of wadding

text: Praying the rosary, counting the prayers on a string of beads. Mademoiselle Gillenormand, too prudish to stay while her nephew is undressed, takes refuge in devotion.
quote: She set herself to telling her beads in her own chamber.

term: “I witnessed the death of Louis XVI”
text: Louis XVI was guillotined on the Place de la Révolution on 21 January 1793. M. Gillenormand, born in the reign of Louis XV and over ninety, has lived through the whole of the Revolution and its sequels, which is why he calls himself a hundred years old.
quote: I witnessed the death of Louis XVI

term: Lafayette, Benjamin Constant, Tirecuir de Corcelles
text: Three liberal deputies of the opposition, the grandfather's villains: Lafayette, the old general of 1789 and 1830; Benjamin Constant, the liberal writer and orator, dead in 1830; and Claude Tircuy de Corcelles, a deputy of the left whose name M. Gillenormand mangles into “Tirecuir” (“Pull-leather”). He blames their speeches for Marius's wounds.
quote: your Lafayettes, your Benjamin Constants, and your Tirecuir de Corcelles

text: Insults from the Revolution: a clubbist was a member of the political clubs such as the Jacobins; the Septembrists were the mobs who massacred prisoners in the Paris jails in September 1792. To M. Gillenormand every young republican is one of them.
quote: Ah! clubbist! Ah! wretch! Ah! Septembrist!

text: Smelling-salts: a phial of ammonia or sal volatile held under the nose to bring someone round from a faint. The grandfather calls it a waste of the doctor's time on a dead boy.
quote: What is the good of making him inhale ammonia and all that parcel of drugs?

term: Two funerals under the same carriage gate
text: In Paris a funeral began at the door of the house, where the coffin lay in state under the carriage entrance hung with black drapery, before the procession left for the church. The grandfather expects to go out the same way as Marius.
quote: That will make two funerals under the same carriage gate.

text: Popular prints fixed two poses of the Emperor: arms folded across the chest, the man of decision, and hands clasped behind the back, the man pondering. Javert had only ever used the first.
quote: Javert had borrowed from Napoleon’s attitudes

term: The Place du Châtelet and its post
text: The square on the right bank opposite the Île de la Cité, on the site of the Grand Châtelet, the medieval fortress that had housed the royal court and prison of Paris until it was demolished in 1802. In 1832 it held a police station-house, marked by its lantern, at the meeting of the quays and the bridges to the Cité.
quote: the post of the Place du Châtelet

term: The rapid by the Pont Notre-Dame
text: Between the Pont Notre-Dame and the Pont au Change, with the Quai de la Mégisserie and the Quai aux Fleurs on either hand, the river ran fast and broken through the arches, worse in 1832 for the piles of a mill built on the bridge. Boatmen dreaded it, and Hugo says the best swimmers drowned there. The river had been swollen by the recent rains.
quote: This point of the Seine is dreaded by mariners.

text: The stone wall, about chest high, that tops the embankment along the Seine, with the drop to the water below. Paris walkers lean their elbows on it to look at the river; it is where Javert stands to think, and where he comes back to.
quote: Javert leaned both elbows on the parapet

text: The Roman governor who handed Jesus over to be crucified and washed his hands before the crowd to show himself innocent of the blood. The voice in Javert's head tells him that arresting the man who saved him would be the same betrayal, with clean hands.
quote: Then have the basin of Pontius Pilate brought and wash your claws.

text: At Fampoux, near Arras, a train on the new Northern Railway left the rails in July 1846 and its carriages fell into a marsh, killing more than a dozen: one of the first great railway disasters in France. Hugo turns Javert into a locomotive running on its rigid line until it leaves the track; the original book title is “Javert Derailed”.
