quote: the Fampoux of a rectilinear conscience

text: Saul of Tarsus, persecutor of Christians, was struck blind by a light from heaven on the road to Damascus and rose as the apostle Paul (Acts 9). Hugo asks whether a locomotive can have such a conversion.
quote: that there should exist for the locomotive a road to Damascus

text: Every police post kept the same furniture for writing reports: a straw-seated chair, a pen, a lead inkstand, a boxwood saucer of sawdust to blot wet ink, and a cardboard box of red wafers to seal the folded sheet. Hugo calls it the lowest stage of official style, where “the literature of the State has its beginning”.
quote: a boxwood saucer filled with sawdust and a wafer box of cardboard filled with red wafers

term: “A few observations for the good of the service”
text: Javert's last report is a list of small abuses in the Paris prisons and the Prefecture: prisoners made to stand barefoot while searched, a chair forbidden at the Madelonettes, bribes to the “barkers” who call names in the visiting room, a contractor's fines in the prison weaving shop, gendarmes gossiping about interrogations. Precise, humane in its details, and sealed like a letter.
quote: A few observations for the good of the service

text: Prisoners given the job of shouting out the names of inmates who had visitors waiting in the parlour. Javert notes that they extorted two sous from each man to call his name clearly.
quote: the prisoners called barkers

text: La Force was the prison in the Marais, in an old ducal mansion, divided into courts named after saints; Sainte-Marie-l’Égyptienne was one of them, used as the visiting parlour. Visitors had to cross the boys' court to reach it.
quote: the parlor of Sainte-Marie-l’Égyptienne

term: The mousetrap of the secret cells
text: The souricière, police slang for the holding cells under the Palais de Justice where prisoners waited to be questioned by the magistrates, kept “in secret”, cut off from all contact. Javert objects that a woman, the canteen-keeper Mme Henry, holds the wicket of so important a place in the Conciergerie.
quote: the wicket to the mousetrap of the secret cells

text: Javert's exact rank, which he gives with his signature, place and hour like any official minute. The police inspectors of Paris were graded in classes, the first being the most senior.
quote: Inspector of the 1st class.

text: Latin legal phrase for a decision not to prosecute; in French procedure, a non-lieu, the examining magistrate's finding that there is no case to answer. Boulatruelle's drunkenness on the night of the Gorbeau ambush left it unclear whether he was a robber or a victim, so he went free.
quote: An order of nolle prosequi

text: Breaking stones for the roads was the work given to ex-convicts and paupers, paid by the state. Boulatruelle, a released galley-convict, lives on the Gagny–Lagny road east of Paris under police surveillance, in a turf-roofed hut.
quote: under administrative supervision, broken stone for the good of the state

text: “Le Capitaine Guillery”, an old popular song about a brigand chief of the early seventeenth century, still whistled by country people. A huntsman's tune in the forest of Montfermeil.
quote: whistling the air of Guillery

text: Virgil's first Eclogue opens on the shepherd Tityrus lying “beneath the shade of a spreading beech”. Hugo's mock-pastoral joke puts the thieving road-mender up the same kind of tree.
quote: a beech-tree of great size, worthy of Tityrus and of Boulatruelle

text: An old name for a glade in a remote, thorny part of the forest of Montfermeil, known to Boulatruelle by its heap of porous stones and a sick chestnut tree bandaged with a sheet of zinc nailed to the bark. Hugo's title calls it “the tree with the zinc plaster”.
quote: This glade was the one which was formerly called the Blaru-bottom.

text: Boulatruelle's joke for a straight line through the thicket, after Napoleon's famously straight Paris street. The straight way through brambles costs him forty minutes.
quote: Let’s take to the wolves’ Rue de Rivoli

term: Chloruretted lotions and nitrate of silver
text: The antiseptics of the 1830s, long before germs were understood. Chlorinated lotions (Labarraque's solution) were used to clean wounds and check rot, and nitrate of silver, lunar caustic, to burn away proud or gangrenous flesh. Marius's healing takes four months.
quote: the chloruretted lotions and the nitrate of silver overcame the gangrene

text: Cloth coated with wax or plaster, used to hold dressings and bandages firmly in place; Hugo notes such fixed dressings were not yet invented in 1832. Without them every dressing had to be bound anew.
quote: the fixation of apparatus and bandages by cerecloths not having been invented as yet

text: After the June rising the Prefect of Police, Gisquet, ordered doctors and hospitals to report every gunshot wound they treated. The order caused an outcry among doctors and public alike, Hugo says the king's included, and it was not enforced, which protected wounded insurgents like Marius.
quote: the inexcusable Gisquet order, which enjoined doctors to lodge information against the wounded

text: A lively old French court dance in duple time, already old-fashioned in 1832. The ninety-year-old dances it alone with finger castanets, singing a gallant song about Jeanne from Fougères in Brittany.
quote: he danced a gavotte, using his thumb and forefinger as castanets

text: Colonel Pontmercy's barony, given by Napoleon on the field of Waterloo and never recognised by the Bourbons, passed in Marius's eyes to his son. The royalist grandfather had always scorned it; calling Marius by it now, like shouting “Long live the Republic!”, shows how far joy has carried him.
quote: He called Marius, “M. le Baron.”

text: The National Convention of 1792–95, which proclaimed the Republic, executed Louis XVI and ran the Terror; Danton, Saint-Just and Robespierre were its leaders. Marius's reply to the royalist harangue is a deliberate challenge, “feeling the ground” before the real battle.
quote: “The men of ’93 were giants,” said Marius with severity.

text: Stock names of French comedy: Dorante is the young gallant, Géronte the old father who stands in the lovers' way. M. Gillenormand, mocking himself, imagines Marius calling him a former beau grown into the obstacle, a mummy “of the Regency and of the Directory”, two famously loose periods of French manners.
quote: that Dorante turned Géronte

term: Taking the cockchafer by the horns
text: The grandfather's comic twist on “taking the bull by the horns”: the cockchafer, or May-beetle, is a clumsy flying beetle children played with. Marius's grand assault turns out to be against a very small beast.
quote: you take the cockchafer by the horns

text: The finest French poet of the 1780s, guillotined under the Terror on 7 Thermidor (25 July 1794), two days before Robespierre fell. His elegy “The Young Invalid” tells of a youth wasting away for love whose mother goes to fetch the girl he loves. The grandfather quotes it, remembers who killed Chénier, and chokes trying to praise the men of ’93 for Marius's sake.
quote: the elegy of the ‘Jeune Malade’ by André Chénier

term: “By the hundred thousand Javottes of the devil”
text: One of M. Gillenormand's invented oaths; Javotte is a typical servant-girl's name. He vents on Basque, polishing boots in the anteroom, the fury he has swallowed in front of Marius.
quote: By the hundred thousand Javottes of the devil

text: Antoine-Marie-Henri Boulard, a Paris notary and the most obsessive book-collector of the age, who filled several houses with hundreds of thousands of volumes and was said never to go out without one. The grandfather's example of a respectable man with a book always under his arm.
quote: Monsieur Boulard, one of my acquaintances, never walked out without a book under his arm

text: M. Gillenormand gets “Fauchelevent” wrong, here and in his other variants. Hugo calls it an aristocratic habit: a great gentleman of the old school did not trouble to remember the names of commoners.
quote: inattention to proper names was an aristocratic habit of his

text: The formal request of marriage, made by the head of the young man's family to the girl's father. Under the Civil Code a son under twenty-five could not marry without the consent of his parents or, failing them, his grandparents, which is why the grandfather's word decides everything. He makes the request with full ceremony, title and all.
quote: I have the honor of asking you, on behalf of my grandson, Baron Marius Pontmercy, for the hand of Mademoiselle.

text: A Catholic married in his own parish church; Saint-Denis du Saint-Sacrement, in the Rue de Turenne, was the Gillenormands'. A dispensation from the parish priest let a wedding take place elsewhere, and the grandfather wants the grander Jesuit church of Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis on the Rue Saint-Antoine, near the old fountain named after Cardinal de Birague.
quote: Our parish is Saint-Denis du Saint Sacrament, but I will get a dispensation so that you can be married at Saint-Paul.

text: Unmarried women of twenty-five or more were said to “coiffer Sainte-Catherine”, to put a cap on the saint's statue on her feast day, 25 November; it meant being an old maid. The grandfather's joke at his spinster daughter's expense, along with the Society of the Virgin, the parish association of unmarried women.
quote: There is a certain Sainte-Catherine whom I should always like to see uncoiffed.

text: “Tower of ivory”, one of the titles of the Virgin Mary in the Litany of Loreto, sung at vespers. For the grandfather it stands for the chill devotions of spinsters.
quote: chanting Turris Eburnea

term: “Alcippe, il est donc vrai, dans peu tu te maries”
text: “So, putting an end to your daydreams, Alcippe, it is true that you will soon be married.” The opening of Boileau's tenth Satire (1694), which goes on to a long attack on women and marriage; the old man quotes the cheerful start and leaves out the rest.
quote: Alcippe, il est donc vrai, dans peu tu te maries.

text: Jean-Baptiste Greuze, eighteenth-century painter of sentimental scenes and of pretty, innocent-looking girls with soft eyes and parted lips. Praise in the language of M. Gillenormand's own youth.
quote: She’s a Greuze.

text: A life annuity (rente viagère): an old man sold most of his capital in return for a fixed income until his death, after which nothing was left to inherit. That is why the grandfather fears Marius and Cosette will have “not a sou” and will be “pulling the devil by the tail”, the French phrase for scraping a living.
quote: More than half of what I possess is swallowed up in an annuity

text: A great fortune: invested in government stock at the usual five percent it would bring some thirty thousand francs a year, enough for a household with carriage and servants, at a time when a working man earned perhaps six or seven hundred a year. The banknotes, five hundred of a thousand francs and the rest of five hundred, were large denominations few people ever saw.
quote: Mademoiselle Euphrasie Fauchelevent possesses six hundred thousand francs.

text: In the old French hierarchy a marquis ranked well above a baron, and a barony from Napoleon counted for little with an old-regime nobleman. The grandfather's compliment is that Cosette looks born to a higher title than the one Marius can give her.
quote: She will only be a Baroness, which is a come down for her; she was born a Marquise.

text: Chérubin is the lovesick page boy of Beaumarchais's Marriage of Figaro; the Rothschilds were the great banking family of Europe, James de Rothschild the richest man in Paris. Love, says the grandfather, has proved a better financier than the banks.
quote: Cherubino works better than Rothschild.

text: Jacques Laffitte, the great Paris banker of the Restoration, whose house in the Rue d’Artois held the fortunes of merchants and industrialists; a liberal, he helped put Louis-Philippe on the throne in 1830 and was briefly his prime minister. Depositors could withdraw on demand with a signed receipt, which is how the money earned at Montreuil-sur-Mer could be taken out in banknotes in a single visit.
quote: to withdraw in season, from the hands of Laffitte, the sum earned by him

text: Shavings of chestnut wood, which resists rot and insects, used as packing to keep the box of banknotes dry in the ground for ten years.
quote: he had placed it in a coffer filled with chestnut shavings

text: Washerwomen of Paris worked on bateaux-lavoirs, big covered barges moored along the quays where they beat linen in the river. The body was found under one, between the Pont au Change and the Pont-Neuf, downstream from where it fell.
quote: found drowned under a boat belonging to some laundresses, between the Pont au Change and the Pont-Neuf

text: Petty, quibbling law work. Marius is a barrister by training; his grandfather, a gentleman of the old school, thinks a baron with money should not plead for fees at all.
quote: don’t go to pettifogging, I beg of you

term: Civil status and the acte de notoriété
text: To marry in France one had to produce one's état civil, the official record of birth and parentage from the town hall. A person without papers could replace it with an acte de notoriété, a sworn statement before a magistrate by witnesses who vouched for who she was. Valjean, an ex-mayor, knows the procedure; the nuns of Petit-Picpus supply the witnesses.
quote: An acte de notoriété was drawn up.

text: Under the Civil Code an orphaned minor had a tuteur, who managed her person and property, and a subrogé tuteur, who watched over the guardian's accounts. Valjean, as “Fauchelevent”, takes the first role and M. Gillenormand the second; the legacy is to be handed over at her majority (twenty-one) or her marriage.
quote: he was appointed, under the name of Fauchelevent, as Cosette’s guardian, with M. Gillenormand as supervising guardian over him

text: The corbeille de mariage: the gifts of clothes, lace, jewels and trinkets that the bridegroom's family presented to the bride before the wedding, often displayed to visitors. M. Gillenormand fills Cosette's from the drawers of three generations of women.
quote: M. Gillenormand was superintending the basket of wedding gifts

term: Binche guipure, Genoa and Alençon point
text: Famous laces: guipure is a heavy lace without a net ground, made at Binche in Hainaut; Genoa and Alençon point were needle-laces, Alençon the “queen of French lace”. Old lace was handed down as family treasure, and it was coming back into fashion.
quote: a robe of Binche guipure which had descended to him from his own grandmother

term: Pekins, lampas, moires, gros de Tours
text: Eighteenth-century silks from the grandfather's drawers: pekin, a striped silk; lampas, a heavily figured silk; moire, watered silk with a rippling sheen; gros de Tours, a ribbed silk from the looms of Tours; dauphines, a light reversible silk. Coromandel lacquer, from the Indian coast, is the black-and-gold lacquer of his chests.
quote: Pekins, damasks, lampas, painted moires, robes of shot gros de Tours

text: Moire antique was a fashionable heavy watered silk. Marius says the men of the Revolution are like an “antique memory”; his grandfather, who will not argue politics now, hears only the name of a dress fabric and orders one.
quote: “Moire antique!” exclaimed the old gentleman.

text: Models of stern republican virtue from antiquity: Cato of Utica, who killed himself rather than live under Caesar, and Phocion, the incorruptible Athenian general put to death by his city. Marius places the men of the Revolution beside them.
quote: like Cato and like Phocion

text: The astronomical clock in Strasbourg cathedral, a tower of dials, planets and moving figures that paraded at noon. Among the figures M. Gillenormand remembers is “Éponine and Sabinus”: the Gaulish rebel Sabinus and his faithful wife Eponina, who hid him in a cave for nine years after a failed rising against Rome. He prefers the clock's useless splendour to the plain Black Forest cuckoo clock.
quote: the Emperor Charles the Fifth, and Éponine, and Sabinus

term: The Duc de Rohan in a tapecu
text: Longchamp was the fashionable promenade where the great showed off their carriages in Holy Week. A tapecu (“bump-bottom”) was a small, plain, jolting cart. For the grandfather, a duke and peer with a string of titles driving there in one, in 1787, signalled the end of the old world.
quote: go to Longchamps in a tapecu

text: Jacques Cujas, the great sixteenth-century jurist, stands for the marriage contract; Camacho is the rich farmer of Don Quixote whose wedding feast, with whole oxen roasting, is the most famous banquet in literature. First the notary, then the feast.
quote: As soon as Cujas had taken his departure, Gamacho entered.

text: An old wedding custom: at the feast the young men contrived to take the bride's garter, which was cut into pieces of ribbon and handed round as favours. The grandfather mourns its passing and makes it the cause of the Trojan War.
quote: I regret the bride’s garter.

text: The rigadoon was a lively old dance. Pierre-Paul Royer-Collard was the grave philosopher-politician of the Doctrinaires, the earnest liberal party of the Restoration, famous for his solemnity. “Your rigadoons are doctrinarian”: even dancing has become serious.
quote: The ideal of an urchin of twenty when he marries, is to resemble M. Royer-Collard.

term: From Rheims to the pagoda of Chanteloup
text: Rheims cathedral was where the kings of France were crowned; the pagoda of Chanteloup, near Amboise, is a Chinese-style folly tower built by the Duc de Choiseul. A wedding, says the grandfather, should run from the sacred to the fanciful.
quote: from the cathedral of Rheims to the pagoda of Chanteloup

text: Amphitrite, sea-goddess and bride of Neptune, was painted riding in a shell-chariot drawn by sea-monsters, with Tritons blowing conch shells: the favourite wedding allegory of eighteenth-century ceilings. The couplet he quotes, about Triton's conch “ravishing whoever heard it”, is a jingle on rhyme alone.
quote: The nuptials of Amphitrite

term: A study required by the council of the order
text: The Order of Barristers of Paris, governed by its council, required a member who wished to practise to have a proper study (cabinet) at his home. Marius had needed one to keep his place at the Bar; his grandfather's library becomes it.
quote: a study, it will be remembered, being required by the council of the order

text: A respectable young woman never went into society, still less to her fiancé's house, without an older relative or protector. Custom also had the suitor call on the bride's family, not the reverse, which is why the aunt grumbles that things are upside down.
quote: Every girl needs a chaperon.

text: A quittance is a receipt showing a debt paid in full. Marius wants to settle two debts of gratitude before he marries: his father's to the sergeant of Waterloo, and his own to the stranger who brought him home.
quote: he wished, before entering joyously into the future, to obtain a quittance from the past

text: A defendant who failed to appear could be tried and sentenced in his absence, par contumace. The sentence stood until he was caught, when he would be retried. The escaped ringleaders of the Gorbeau ambush got hard labour for life, the chief death; only two minor accomplices, present in the dock, got ten years.
quote: Thénardier, the head and leader, had been, through contumacy, likewise condemned to death.

term: Died in prison pending the trial
text: Accused persons could be held for many months in preventive detention before the Assizes sat, and prisons such as Saint-Lazare and La Force were unhealthy places. Death before trial ended the case against that defendant.
quote: Madame Thénardier had died in prison pending the trial.

text: The Prefecture of Police kept registers of every arrest and the agents' written reports. Since no report of an arrest at the sewer outlet on 6 June was ever filed, the Prefecture treats the coachman's story as a fable invented in the hope of a tip. Marius has to inquire discreetly, being himself a former insurgent.
quote: They had no knowledge of any arrest having been made on the 6th of June at the mouth of the Grand Sewer.

text: Writing in the 1860s, Hugo mocks the newly imported English fashion of the couple leaving straight from church in a hired post-chaise for a wedding journey and a night at an inn, with the crack of the postilion's whip (the “clic-clacs”). In 1833 a French couple still married and spent the wedding night at home.
quote: France had not yet borrowed from England that supreme delicacy of carrying off one’s wife

text: Adolphe Adam's comic opera of 1836, whose hero is a dashing coach-driver in blue jacket, leather breeches, powdered hair and tall boots. Hugo's sneer: modern weddings need a postilion as well as the mayor and the priest.
quote: the Postilion de Lonjumeau

term: Old shoes after the bridal carriage
text: The English custom of throwing old shoes and slippers after a newly married couple for luck. Hugo attaches a story to it about John Churchill, later Duke of Marlborough (the “Malbrouck” of the French nursery song), pelted on his wedding day by an angry aunt.
quote: a hail storm of slippers trodden down at heel and of worn-out shoes

text: Since 1792 French marriage had been a civil act: banns posted at the town hall, papers checked, and the marriage pronounced by the mayor in his tricolour scarf. A Catholic couple then went to church for the religious ceremony, which had no legal force by itself. Hence the delay until 16 February.
quote: the banns to publish, the papers to be drawn up, the mayoralty, and the church

text: Shrove Tuesday (Mardi Gras, “fat Tuesday”), the last day of Carnival before the fast of Lent, fell on 16 February in 1833. It was the great day of masks in Paris: carriages and wagons of masqueraders paraded along the boulevards between the Madeleine and the Bastille, and crowds lined the way. A wedding on that day was unusual, and Aunt Gillenormand has scruples.
quote: it chanced that the 16th fell on Shrove Tuesday

term: “Mariage un Mardi gras n’aura point enfants ingrats”
text: “A marriage on Shrove Tuesday will have no ungrateful children.” A rhyming country proverb, which the grandfather produces at once to overrule his daughter.
quote: Mariage un Mardi gras

text: The default marriage regime of the Civil Code: the couple's goods and income formed one common fund managed by the husband. With no special marriage contract needed, “the papers had been simple”, and the money became, in law, Marius's to administer.
quote: As the marriage was taking place under the regime of community of property, the papers had been simple.

text: The guardian of a minor bride had to sign the marriage register at the town hall and the deed handing over her property. With his right hand bandaged in a sling, “M. Fauchelevent” cannot sign; M. Gillenormand, as supervising guardian, signs in his place.
quote: had prevented his signing

text: Stock characters of the Carnival, from Italian comedy and the fair: Merry-Andrew is the buffoon, Pantaloon the old Venetian merchant, Harlequin and Columbine the lovers, Cassandre the duped old father, Janot the simpleton of the boulevard theatres. Parisians dressed as them in the streets, children too.
quote: Merry-Andrew, Pantaloon and Clown persisted

text: Kinds of Paris carriage: the citadine was a light hired cab, the tapissière an open-sided delivery van used for outings, the cariole a small country cart. On Shrove Tuesday they all joined the slow procession up and down the boulevards, kept in two files by the police.
quote: citadines, tapissières, carioles, cabriolets marching in order

text: The “fat ox”: a prize ox, garlanded and ridden by a child dressed as Cupid, paraded through Paris by the butchers at Carnival with music and a procession before it went to slaughter. It had the right of way in the middle of the boulevard with the carriages of peers and ambassadors.
quote: notably that of the Boeuf Gras

text: Lord Henry Seymour, a rich Anglo-French sportsman and founder of the Jockey Club in Paris, notorious for his Carnival extravagances. The crowd's nickname for him was “Milord l'Arsouille”, Lord Rowdy.
quote: Lord Seymour’s post-chaise, harassed by a nickname from the populace, passed with great noise

text: The point on the boulevard near the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire where an old bridge over the Marais drain had once stood, at the end of the Rue du Pont-aux-Choux. It is where the two files of carriages stop side by side.
quote: At the top of the Pont-aux-Choux, there was a stoppage.

term: The chariot of Thespis and the hackney-coach of Vadé
text: Thespis, the legendary first actor of Greece, was said to tour with his players in a cart; Vadé was the eighteenth-century poet of the fishmarket, inventor of the “poissard” style in the slang of the Halles. Hugo's pair: Greek tragedy began on a wagon, Paris low comedy rides in a cab.
quote: Greece stood in need of the chariot of Thespis, France stands in need of the hackney-coach of Vadé.

text: French for “wolf”: a black half-mask of velvet or satin covering the eyes and upper face, the usual disguise at masked balls. The young fishwife wears one with her low-necked gown in the February rain.
quote: masked with a loup

term: “I owe my fishwife day to the prefecture”
text: Hugo's charge is that the Prefecture of Police hired people, many from the shady margins of Paris, to ride in the masqueraders' wagons and keep up the Carnival. The girl is paid for the day, watched by inspectors, and cannot leave the cart without risking arrest.
quote: I owe my fishwife day to the prefecture.

text: The first day of Lent, when Carnival ends and the faithful receive ashes on the forehead. After Shrove Tuesday masks disappear from the streets, so a man who goes about only in disguise loses his cover.
quote: It’s Ash Wednesday.

text: Where Paris weddings went to feast: the Cadran-Bleu was a famous restaurant on the Boulevard du Temple, and the Quai de la Rapée, up the river by the wine depots, was lined with taverns serving fried fish. The girl's guesses are the obvious ones.
quote: To the Cadran-Bleu.

text: The white wedding dress was still fairly new as a custom in 1833, a fashion of the Restoration. Cosette's is the full set: white taffeta petticoat, the heirloom Binche guipure, a veil of English point lace, pearls, and the wreath of orange blossom, the emblem of a virgin bride.
quote: a wreath of orange flowers

text: Paul Barras, the most powerful of the five Directors who governed France from 1795 to 1799, presided over a society of gamblers, speculators and extravagantly dressed dandies. The grandfather's finery belongs to that age.
quote: all the elegances of the epoch of Barras

term: The pall of white moire and the suisse
text: During the nuptial blessing a square of cloth, the poêle, was held over the kneeling couple. The suisse was the church's ceremonial officer, originally a Swiss guard, in a uniform with epaulets, a cocked hat and a halberd, who led processions and kept order, tapping the pavement as he walked.
quote: preceded by the suisse, with the epaulets of a colonel, tapping the pavement with his halberd

text: What the fortune yields at about five percent, which the old man still counts in livres (by then the same as francs). It was the income of a rich household with carriage and servants, many times what a government clerk earned in a year.
quote: with an income of thirty thousand livres

text: Cosette plays on tu and vous. Lovers and married couples said tu, “thou”, to each other in private; in public it was still vous. Now that they are married, she is “Madame Tu”.
quote: I am Madame Thou.

text: A lustre is a chandelier; a Venetian one is of Murano glass, here with little coloured glass birds among the candles. Girandoles are branched candlesticks, often with mirror backs or hanging prisms. Hundreds of candles made the dining room “as brilliant as the daylight”.
quote: a Venetian lustre with flat plates

text: The shepherd lovers of Florian's pastoral romance Estelle et Némorin (1788), sweetness itself. The grandfather mocks the philosophers who would tell even such lovers to be moderate.
quote: Take care, Estelle, thou art too pretty! Have a care, Nemorin, thou art too handsome!

text: A famous diamond of the French crown jewels, named after Nicolas de Harlay de Sancy, who owned it under Henri III and Henri IV. Hugo's French puns on its weight, “cent six” carats sounding like Sancy; the English “six hundred carats” misses the joke (the real stone weighs about fifty-five).
quote: Is the Sancy diamond called the Sancy because it belonged to Harley de Sancy, or because it weighs six hundred carats?

term: Trip-gallant and cholera-morbus; pourrée and cachuca
text: The grandfather says the young think they have changed the world only by renaming things. “Trousse-galant” was the old popular name for a deadly summer fever, and the modern one is cholera; the bourrée was an old country dance, and its successor the Spanish cachucha, the rage in Paris in the 1830s.
quote: your trip-gallant is called the cholera-morbus, and because your pourrée is called the cachuca

text: The flirtatious young widow and her gruff lover in Molière's The Misanthrope. The grandfather makes the planet Venus the coquette and the stormy ocean the misanthrope who smiles in spite of himself.
quote: the Célimène of the ocean

term: Daphnis and Chloe, Philemon and Baucis
text: Two pairs of classical lovers: Daphnis and Chloe, the young shepherd sweethearts of Longus's Greek romance, and Philemon and Baucis, the old couple in Ovid who are granted their wish to die at the same moment and become two trees. Young love first, faithful old age afterwards.
quote: Be Daphnis and Chloe, while waiting to become Philemon and Baucis.

term: The great prize in the lottery
text: The state lottery, with its weekly draws and huge prizes, was a passion of the Parisian poor until it was abolished in 1836. The grandfather tells the couple they have drawn the winning number.
quote: You have filched the winning number in the lottery

term: Ventre-saint-gris and the oaths of the grandfather
text: Ventre-saint-gris (“by the grey saint's belly”) was Henri IV's favourite oath, and the good-living king was remembered for food, wine and women. Saperlotte, sarpejou, ventregoulette and vertu-bamboche are old-fashioned mock oaths of the kind M. Gillenormand delights in.
quote: Ventre-saint-gris!

text: Le Bonhomme Jadis, a one-act comedy by Henri Murger (1852) about a kindly old man who brings two young people together. Hugo says the play's old-fashioned spirit was present at the wedding in M. Gillenormand.
quote: Goodman Days of Yore might have been invited to it.

text: Black coat, knee-breeches, white stockings and white gloves: the full dress of a manservant waiting at a grand dinner, in the old style that M. Gillenormand keeps up in his household.
quote: Basque, in a black coat, knee-breeches, white stockings and white gloves

text: Fustian is a thick, hard-wearing twilled cloth of cotton and linen, used for working clothes and children's garments; ticking is the striped cotton that covers mattresses and pillows. A bare pillow in its ticking, without a case, marks a bed stripped and left empty.
quote: the fustian bodice, which was very thick

text: Even small children were dressed in black for a dead parent, for a year or more. The black dress, fichu, shoes and stockings Valjean brought to Montfermeil in 1823 were mourning clothes for her dead mother.
quote: to clothe herself in these mourning habiliments

text: In Genesis 32 Jacob wrestles all night with a mysterious stranger, is lamed at the hip, and will not let go until he is blessed. Hugo's point: Jacob fought once; Valjean has fought his conscience many nights.
quote: Jacob struggled with the angel but one night.

text: In Greek myth the Danaids, who murdered their husbands, are condemned in the underworld to fill a jar that has a hole in the bottom; Sisyphus forever rolls his stone uphill. Hugo's images of a conscience that asks for everything and is never full.
quote: Somewhere in the fog of the ancient hells, there is a tun like that.

text: A pun from chemistry: sublimation is turning a solid into vapour by heat, and “corrosive sublimate” was mercuric chloride, a deadly poison. Martyrdom, Hugo says, both raises a man up and eats him away.
quote: Martyrdom is sublimation, corrosive sublimation.

term: The throne and crown of red-hot iron
text: A torture of legend and history: the Hungarian peasant rebel György Dózsa, captured in 1514, was set on a red-hot iron throne and crowned with a red-hot crown in mockery of his claim to be king. Hugo extends it to sceptre, orb and a mantle of flame.
quote: one seats oneself on the throne of glowing iron

text: Servants of a titled house took pride in announcing “Monsieur le Baron”, Hugo says, because some of the title splashed onto them. The barony is Napoleon's grant to Colonel Pontmercy; the republican Marius uses it only because his father's last wish told him to, while the royalist grandfather now clings to it.
quote: they are what a philosopher would call, bespattered with the title

term: The voyages of Cook and Vancouver
text: The narratives of Captain James Cook's Pacific voyages and of George Vancouver's survey of the north-west coast of America, popular reading in French translation. They are among the few books on M. Fauchelevent's shelf, books of distant journeys for a man who never travels.
quote: your Voyages of Captain Cook and the other—Vancouver’s

text: The English card game for four, ancestor of bridge, the fashionable evening game of elderly gentlemen in the salons of the 1830s. Marius offers it as the way to delight his grandfather.
quote: Do you play whist?

term: “The days when I am at the courts”
text: Marius means to practise as a barrister at the Palais de Justice, pleading cases before the courts, now that he has a study at home and a family. A barrister of the Paris Bar went daily to the Palais in his gown.
quote: on the days when I am at the courts

text: To sign the marriage register or the guardianship deeds with a name not one's own was a forgery in a public document (faux en écriture publique), a serious crime that could also have made the marriage papers open to challenge. Valjean's bandaged thumb was invented so that only true names went into the record.
quote: I invented this injury in order that I might not commit a forgery, that I might not introduce a flaw into the marriage documents

term: “Our oath to others may not be received in law”
text: A man sentenced to hard labour suffered civil degradation: among other losses of rights, he could never again give sworn testimony in a court, only “information”. Valjean asks Marius to believe a word that the law would not accept.
quote: although our oath to others may not be received in law

term: Condemned for life for a second offence
text: The penal code punished repeat offenders far more heavily. A released convict who broke his ban (left the town assigned to him with his yellow passport) and stole again could be sent back to the galleys for life, which is what Valjean now tells Marius he is under.
quote: Then, I was condemned for life for theft, for a second offence. At the present moment, I have broken my ban.

text: A phrase from the criminal courts: the reform of the penal code in 1832 allowed juries to find “extenuating circumstances” and so lower a sentence. Valjean speaks of his care for Cosette in the language of a man in the dock.
quote: Register this attenuating circumstance.

term: The diligences of the Rue Bouloy
text: The Rue du Bouloi, near the Palais-Royal, held the offices of the great stage-coach companies, from which the diligences left for the provinces. To go away for good, Valjean need only walk there.
quote: there are diligences in the Rue Bouloy

text: Invisible ink, made from lemon juice, milk or certain chemicals, whose writing appears only when the paper is warmed. Hugo's image for the memory of the barricade surfacing in Marius under the heat of emotion.
quote: like sympathetic ink at the application of heat

text: The blood feud of Corsica, where a family's honour required killing whoever had killed or wronged one of its own, generation after generation. Mérimée's story Colomba (1840) made it famous in France. Marius explains to himself what he heard behind the Mondétour barricade as a convict's vengeance of this kind.
quote: The Corsican vendetta has penetrated to certain lower strata and has become the law there

text: The first two sons of Adam in Genesis: Abel, the keeper of sheep whose offering pleased God, and Cain, who killed him and was marked and sent out to wander. Marius cannot fit the man he sees into the old pattern: “What was this tender Cain?”
quote: the one which is according to good is Abel; the other which is according to evil is Cain

text: French distinguishes la loi, the written statute, from le droit, right or justice. In the penal thinking of the day a convict suffered civil degradation and, for life sentences, “civil death”: he lost his legal existence, could not inherit, make a will or validly marry. Marius, a democrat in politics, still accepts this as civilisation.
quote: He had not yet come to distinguish between that which is written by man and that which is written by God, between law and right.

text: Latin, “Get thee behind me”, from Christ's rebuke in the Gospels (“Vade retro, Satana”) and the formula of exorcism. Marius's final inward gesture towards the convict.
quote: Vade retro.

text: A round brush on a long pole for sweeping cobwebs from ceilings and high corners; in French a tête-de-loup, “wolf's head”, rendered here as “pope's head”. The room Valjean chooses is one that never sees it.
quote: the pope’s head brush

text: A father said tu, “thou”, to his daughter, and she called him “father”. By saying vous and “Madame”, and asking to be called “Monsieur Jean”, Valjean speaks to Cosette as a servant or a stranger would speak to a married lady. When he slips back into “thou”, she hears it at once.
quote: “You know, madame, that I am peculiar, I have my freaks.”

text: A dressing table with mirror and drawers, veneered in the dark, red-streaked tropical wood fashionable under Charles X and Louis-Philippe, often with pale inlay. Valjean, offered love, answers with shopping advice.
quote: A very neat toilet table in the reigning style. What you call rosewood, I think.

text: A nobleman of anecdote whose eccentricity, as the grandfather tells it, was to buy a palace and live in its garret. For M. Gillenormand such “originals” are common, and M. Fauchelevent's insistence on the cellar room is one more harmless whim.
quote: The Marquis de Canaples was still worse. He bought a palace that he might lodge in the garret.

term: One's candle at the porter's lodge
text: Tenants of a Paris house left their bedroom candlestick and key with the porter and collected them on coming home at night to light their way up the stairs. A rich man who does so, and comes in by the side door, is living like a poor lodger: one of Hugo's “fugitive folds on the surface”.
quote: having one’s key in one’s pocket, and one’s candle at the porter’s lodge, however rich one may be

term: Arguing a case here and there
text: Marius has begun to practise at the Bar, taking a brief now and then. A young barrister without connections pleaded small cases, or was assigned the defence of the poor; with a fortune behind him he need not chase work.
quote: Marius argued a case here and there

text: The house in the Rue Plumet had been rented, not bought, on a lease that still ran, in Cosette's name. So the couple can still go back to its garden.
quote: The house in the Rue Plumet being held on a lease, still belonged to Cosette.

term: A coupé, a maid and a box at the theatre
text: The marks of a rich young household in 1833: a coupé (a closed two-seat carriage) with horses and coachman, a lady's maid, a house of one's own and a box for the season at the Opéra or the Théâtre-Italien. Valjean, who has given them a fortune, sees them walking and taking hackney cabs and living with the grandfather on one servant.
quote: Why do you not have a carriage of your own?

text: Marius's sum: twenty-seven thousand livres a year from Cosette's fortune and three thousand from his grandfather's allowance. Three thousand francs was a modest middle-class income, enough for a small flat and a maid but no carriage. His question whether she could live on it alone tells Valjean what Marius thinks of the money.
quote: Twenty-seven that you own, and three that my grandfather gives me.

text: Wallflowers (giroflées) and snapdragons, the plants that seed themselves in the cracks of old walls and bloom in early spring. Hugo fills the old garden walls of the Marais with them in April.
quote: a jewelled garniture of gillyflowers spread over the ancient walls

term: From the Rue de l’Homme Armé to the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire
text: A walk of a quarter of an hour north through the Marais: past the Blancs-Manteaux, up the Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, left at the Rue de l’Écharpe into the long Rue Saint-Louis, which runs to the corner of the Filles-du-Calvaire. Hugo names each street as the walk shrinks: the Rue Pavée, the Rue des Trois-Pavillons, and at last no farther than the Blancs-Manteaux.
quote: passed in front of the Blancs Manteaux, gained the Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine

text: In the old sense, a simpleton or harmless half-wit, “God's innocent”. The women of the quarter take the old man who stops at a corner and weeps for one, and the children laugh at him.
quote: The good women of the quarter said: “He is an innocent.”

text: The porter's wife, who in many Paris houses cooked and cleaned for single lodgers for a few sous, besides keeping the door and the stairs. She is the only person Valjean sees. Her cabbage and potatoes with bacon, and her pride in her “ladyfinger” potatoes (a long, waxy variety), are poor people's fare.
quote: His portress, who prepared his scanty repasts, a few cabbages or potatoes with bacon

text: A French way of saying “never”, from the nursery song of Malbrough, who “will come back at Easter, or at Trinity”, and never does. The portress means she does not believe his promise to eat tomorrow.
quote: “Or at Trinity day. Why not today?

term: “That gibbet is always good to look at”
text: Hugo's name for the crucifix: the cross was the gallows of the Roman world, and Christ died on it between two thieves. A man condemned by the law hangs one opposite his bed.
quote: That gibbet is always good to look at.

text: In a house of mourning, candles were kept burning beside a body lying in its room, day and night, until the burial. Hugo points out the custom himself: lighting the Bishop's candlesticks in summer daylight is a deathbed sign.
quote: In the same way candles are to be seen lighted in broad daylight in chambers where there is a corpse.

term: Writing with the back of the pen
text: A quill pen left unused dried and its split nib curled; the ink in the pot dried to a crust. With no strength to mend the quill with a penknife, Valjean thins the ink with water and writes with the back of the nib.
quote: he was compelled to write with the back of the pen

term: Gum shellac and the jet wax
text: The secret of the fortune, set down in figures: imitation jet and black-glass beads were fixed to their metal settings with a wax that had been made of resin and lampblack at four livres the pound. Replacing it with shellac (a resin from an Indian insect) and turpentine at thirty sous, a seventh of the price and better, is the invention that made the black-bead trade of Montreuil-sur-Mer rich.
quote: I invented a way of making it with gum shellac and turpentine.

text: Distilled alcohol, burned in a small lamp to give a clean, steady flame. The bead-maker needs one to soften the wax as he works at his tiny anvil.
quote: a lamp burning spirits of wine to soften the wax

term: Baron Thénard, member of the Institute
text: Louis-Jacques Thénard, the eminent chemist (discoverer of hydrogen peroxide and of “Thénard's blue”), made a baron by Charles X and a member of the Académie des Sciences, part of the Institut de France. The letter-writer borrows the famous name, his own “a trifle abridged”.
quote: I might have been baron Thénard, member of the Institute

text: Hôtel in French also means a private town mansion, as in hôtel particulier. Addressing a letter to a baron “at his hotel” was the grand style; the spelling “Pommerci” and the coarse paper give the writer away.
quote: “To Monsieur, Monsieur le Baron Pommerci. At his hotel.”

text: Hugo's account of an old-clothes man near the Arsenal who hired out respectable costumes to thieves at thirty sous a day: a magistrate's suit, a priest's, a banker's, a retired officer's, and the black “ex-ambassador” outfit with wig, green spectacles, watch-seals and two little quills to change the shape of the nose. The clothes always came back, and never fitted.
quote: This costumer was called “the Changer;”

text: William Pitt the Younger, the famously thin British prime minister, and the Prince of Castelcicala, the Neapolitan ambassador in Paris, apparently notable for his bulk. The statesman's suit fits neither, and certainly not the man wearing it.
quote: too large for Pitt and too small for Castelcicala

text: Grand names to drop: Princess Bagration, widow of a Russian general, kept a famous salon in Paris; Dambray had been Chancellor of France under the Restoration; Chateaubriand was the greatest writer and royalist statesman of the age. The visitor claims to have met Marius in all their drawing-rooms.
quote: at the house of Madame la Princesse Bagration and in the drawing-rooms of his Lordship the Vicomte Dambray

text: The visitor's tale of a fortified village of adobe near Panama, a single terraced block entered by ladders, in gold country. Panama was then a province of New Granada (Colombia), a crossing-place between the oceans. It is the destination he names for the money he wants.
quote: There is in America, in a district near Panama, a village called la Joya.

text: Prescription: under French criminal law, prosecution for a crime lapsed after ten years, and an unexecuted sentence after twenty, so that very old deeds could no longer be punished. The visitor stresses that his “secret” concerns crimes too recent to be covered.
quote: deeds of the past which have lapsed, which can be effaced by limitation before the law and by repentance before God

text: The visitor's slang for the five-hundred-franc banknote flung in his face, which rustles as it is handled; the joke is that it is the only honest thing in the room.
quote: “An honest rustler.”

term: A protested bill and the debtors' prison
text: A letter of change (bill of exchange) was a written order to pay; when the debtor failed to pay, the creditor had it formally “protested” before a notary, and could have him jailed in the debtors' prison, at Paris the prison of Clichy. Marius sees his father's dying wish as a bill drawn on him that he has not yet honoured.
quote: the letter of change drawn from the depths of the tomb by his father upon him, Marius, had been protested up to that day

text: The Moniteur universel was the official government newspaper; communications from the Prefecture of Police were printed in it as fact. That is why Marius cannot doubt what it reports of the inspector's death and of the verbal report he made to the Prefect.
quote: the note printed in the Moniteur had been an administrative communication from the Prefecture of Police

text: A banker's draft, a written order payable by a correspondent bank in New York. Paying the twenty thousand francs that way meant the money could be collected only after the man had sailed: Marius's way of making sure he goes.
quote: furnished with a draft on New York for twenty thousand francs

text: The Atlantic slave trade had been outlawed by Britain and the United States, but slavery remained legal in the American South, in Brazil and in Cuba until the 1860s and after, and smuggling and the internal trade went on. Hugo, a fierce abolitionist, gives that trade to his worst villain.
quote: With Marius’ money, Thénardier set up as a slave-dealer.

text: Berlin iron jewellery, delicate cast-iron necklaces and bracelets, was famous after Prussian women gave their gold for the war of 1813 and wore iron instead. A gross is twelve dozen, 144 pieces. The dying man's figures (buckles costing ten francs the gross and selling for sixty) are his proof that the fortune was honestly made.
quote: We rivalled what is called Berlin jewellery.

text: A dying Catholic was expected to receive the last sacraments, confession and extreme unction, from a priest, and the portress offers to fetch one as any neighbour would. The answer points elsewhere.
quote: “Would you like a priest?”

text: Graves of the comfortable bore inscribed names and dates; the poor went into the common trench or under an unmarked stone. To ask for the first plot of earth found, and no name, is to ask to be buried as a poor man.
quote: No name on the stone.

text: Père-Lachaise, the great cemetery on the eastern hill of Paris, had its fashionable quarter of chapels and monuments and, at its edges, the fosse commune, the trenches where the poor were buried free and their bones later cleared. The plain stone lies near it, under a yew, off any path.
quote: in the vicinity of the common grave

term: “Il dort. Quoique le sort fût pour lui bien étrange”
text: The four pencilled lines: “He sleeps. Although fate was very strange for him, he lived. He died when he had his angel no more. It came about simply, of itself, as night falls when day goes.” Alexandrines, the classic verse of French epitaphs, written by an unknown hand and already washed away.
quote: Il dort. Quoique le sort fût pour lui bien étrange
